false_positives.candidate:
Delete-cache action shown for delegation/team credentials that the handler rejects

deleteCacheHandler authorizes solely by `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. Delegation credentials (and team credentials with a null userId) are owned by a different user/admin, so this lookup returns null and the mutation throws "Credential not found or access denied". However, CredentialActionsDropdown only hides the remove-app action for delegation (`canDisconnect = !delegationCredentialId && ...`); it still renders the "Delete cached data" action whenever `hasCache` is truthy, and delegated Google calendars do have a cache row keyed by that credential's DB id, so `cacheUpdatedAt` is set. Result: delegated/team users see "Delete cached data" but every attempt fails with the error toast. Either authorize using the same rule that builds connectedCalendars, or hide the delete action when the credential isn't owned by the session user.

Deleting cache does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status

deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess only calls `onSuccess?.()` (= props.onChanged). Unlike disconnectMutation, which explicitly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in onSettled, the cache mutation never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. When the parent does not pass a refetching `onChanged` (it is optional in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper), the tRPC cache retains the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so after a successful delete the dropdown still shows "Cache Status" and "Delete cached data" until a manual page reload. Invalidate the connectedCalendars query in onSuccess/onSettled as the disconnect path does.

Migration backfills all existing caches with the migration timestamp

Adding `updatedAt TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` sets every pre-existing CalendarCache row to the migration run time. getCacheStatusByCredentialIds surfaces this value as "Last updated", so for the existing rows the UI will report the deploy time as the last update for up to the cache TTL (CACHING_TIME = 30 days), which is misleading. Since the real update time can be approximated as `expiresAt - CACHING_TIME`, consider backfilling with that (or leaving the column nullable for legacy rows) instead of NOW().

No test for deleteCache authorization ceiling

deleteCache permanently deletes calendar cache rows and its only safety property is the ownership check. There is no test asserting that a user cannot delete the cache of a credential they do not own (mutation should reject) and can delete their own. Given this is a destructive, authorization-gated mutation, a unit/integration test covering the not-owner rejection and the owner success path should be added before merge.

Unnecessary SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update with no reader

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now ends with `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`. This issues an extra UPDATE across all SelectedCalendars for the credential on every cache population (i.e. every sync/webhook), only to bump `@updatedAt`, yet nothing reads SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for display — the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt via cacheUpdatedAt. The PR notes this too. It is dead work on a latency-sensitive path; remove it (or add the consumer that justifies it).

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation promises are not awaited

In the reminder-cancellation loop, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async but are invoked inside `updatedBookings.forEach(...).forEach(...)` without `await`ing them, and the resulting promises are never collected or awaited. For EMAIL reminders the only thing that prevents delivery is the `cancelled: true` DB write performed inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`; if that floating promise has not completed when the handler returns (likely on serverless, where the lambda can be frozen right after the response is sent), the reminder stays scheduled and the email is still delivered — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. Collect and `await Promise.all(...)` all cancellation promises before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves orphan WorkflowReminder rows

When `immediateDelete` is true the function cancels the send in SendGrid and returns, but it never deletes the `workflowReminder` row nor marks it `cancelled`. Callers in `handleNewBooking` (reschedule) no longer perform a separate `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany`, so for a rescheduled booking the old reminders remain in the table as `scheduled: true` rows referencing the cancelled booking until the cron's past-reminder cleanup eventually deletes them. Delete the row here (or set `cancelled`) so the DB state matches the actual SendGrid state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Past-reminder cleanup deletes cancelled reminders before they can be cancelled

The handler first runs `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` and only afterwards looks up `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Because the cleanup runs first, any cancelled reminder whose `scheduledDate` has just passed is deleted from the DB without ever being cancelled in SendGrid, so the reminder email is delivered. Since this cron runs every 15 minutes, a cancellation made within ~15 minutes of a reminder's send time (after the last cron run while the reminder was still in the future) falls into this gap and the email goes out. The cancellation pass should run before/independent of the past-reminder cleanup, and the window/cadence must guarantee every reminder is cancelled before its send time.

Reschedule reminder cleanup: try/catch is dead code and calls are unawaited

The new reschedule cleanup wraps the loop in `try { originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) }) } catch (error) { log.error(...) }`. The callback is async and its promises are not awaited, so (a) any rejection from the cancellation calls becomes an unhandled rejection and is never caught by this `catch`, making the error handling dead code, and (b) the SendGrid cancellation / DB update may not complete before the handler finishes, so reminders for the old (now rescheduled) booking can still be sent. Additionally, passing `immediateDelete=true` for email performs an immediate SendGrid `status: cancel` POST, which is exactly the pending-cancellation behaviour (max 100 entries in `scheduled_sends`) this PR is trying to avoid, so reschedule-heavy accounts can still exhaust that limit and fail to cancel. Await the calls and consider using the mark-cancelled path for reschedules too.

requestReschedule reminder cancellation not awaited

In `requestReschedule`, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are called inside `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` without awaiting. For EMAIL these functions only mark the row `cancelled: true`, so if the floating promise does not run before the request completes (serverless freeze), the reminder for the now-cancelled/rescheduled booking stays live and the reminder email is still sent — the bug being fixed. Await or `Promise.all` these calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach in reschedule is not awaited and try/catch cannot catch its failures

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` starts async callbacks but does not await the returned promises. `Reschedule` can return before `getCalendar` and `deleteEvent` finish, and the surrounding try/catch is ineffective for rejections from those awaits, producing unhandled rejections and potentially leaving calendar events undeleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` or a `for...of` loop.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are initiated eagerly, so app loading is not actually lazy

Each `import("./...")` call in the object literal is evaluated as soon as `packages/app-store/index.ts` is imported. That starts loading/evaluating every app chunk immediately, so this change does not defer app loading and can still pay the full startup cost. If the goal is lazy loading, store thunks such as `() => import("./app")` and call/await only the selected app.

Recurring cancellation may skip calendar deletes because async forEach is not awaited

In the recurring-bookings branch, credentials are processed with `forEach(async ...)`. The callback awaits `getCalendar` and only then pushes deletion promises into `apiDeletes`, but the outer handler does not await the callbacks. It may reach `await Promise.all(...apiDeletes)` before those deletions are pushed, leaving recurring calendar events undeleted, and callback rejections become unhandled. Convert this to an awaited `for...of` loop or `Promise.all` over the credentials.

appStore export now returns promises while most consumers still expect modules

The default export was changed from a map of module namespaces to a map of `import()` promises. Every existing `appStore[name]` access now yields a Promise unless the caller awaits it. This PR updates only a small set of call sites, so other consumers will read `.lib`, `.metadata`, or `.credentials` from a Promise and get undefined, breaking calendar, video, and payment integrations at runtime (and likely failing typecheck where the old module type is expected). Either keep a synchronous metadata map or update every consumer and the exported type to the async contract.

getCalendarCredentials now silently returns calendar promises

Because `getCalendar` became async, `getCalendarCredentials` now stores a `Promise<Calendar | null>` in the `calendar` field while remaining a synchronous function. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await that field. Any other caller of this exported function that treats `calendar` as a Calendar will call methods on a Promise. Make the function async and await `getCalendar`, or explicitly change the return type to expose promises and migrate all callers.

requestReschedule fires calendar deletion asynchronously without awaiting it

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside an async callback that the mutation never awaits. The mutation can return before calendar/video cleanup starts or completes, and failures become unhandled rejections rather than being handled by the mutation. Collect the promises with `map` and `await Promise.all` so reschedule cleanup is reliable.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check mishandles days off and split shifts

The new working-hours guard uses workingHours.find and returns false only when the first entry whose days includes slotStartTime.day() does not contain the slot. This has two failure modes: (1) if the user has no working-hours entry for that weekday, find returns undefined and the slot falls through as available, so fixed hosts can be booked on their days off; (2) if the user has multiple ranges on the same weekday, such as 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00, an afternoon slot is compared only against the first range and rejected even though it is within the second range. In addition, line 142 sets end equal to start instead of using slotEndTime, so a slot that starts before closing but ends after closing is not rejected. The check needs to reject missing weekday entries and test the slot against all matching ranges, including the slot end.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date override interval only rejects slots wholly before or after it

The containment test rejects a slot only when slotEndTime is before/equal overrideStart or slotStartTime is after overrideEnd. It therefore accepts slots that partially overlap an override: a 13:30-14:30 slot with a 14:00-18:00 override starts before the override but ends inside and is treated as within the override; a slot starting exactly at 18:00 is also accepted because the end check uses strict isAfter. Combined with the early return on dateOverrideExist, these slots bypass normal working hours and busy checks. The condition should require slotStartTime >= overrideStart and slotEndTime <= overrideEnd. Separately, the zero-length override check at line 114 compares two Dayjs objects with ===, so a start-equals-end override is never recognized as the unavailable case.

false_positives.candidate:
Active date overrides are still selected by the override wall-clock UTC date

activeOverrides is selected by comparing dayjs.utc(override.start) directly against the invitee's local day boundaries. Date override start values are stored as wall-clock times (for example, 14:00 Asia/Kolkata is stored as 14:00Z), so this comparison works only when the organizer and invitee dates happen to align. For a large positive invitee offset such as UTC+14, an override stored at 14:00Z on the invitee day falls after the invitee day's UTC end boundary (10:00Z the same day), so the override is filtered out and the new timezone conversion is never applied. The filter should compare the converted instant or otherwise test overlap against the invitee day.

Date override path returns true before busy-time checks

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot falls inside a date override the function sets dateOverrideExist and then returns true at line 133 before the busy.every(...) check at line 153. The busy array contains the host's Cal bookings and calendar busy times. As a result, any fixed host with a date override appears free for the whole override even when already booked, so personal and round-robin events can create double bookings on override days. The override should bypass normal working-hour checks only; busy times still need to be evaluated.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin date override fix

The PR description says fixed-host date overrides in round-robin events are fixed and should prevent bookings when the fixed host is unavailable, but the added test only changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It has no ROUND_ROBIN event, no fixed host with a date override, and no busy booking on the override day. As a result, the regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (busy times being skipped and the working-hours filtering) are not caught. Add a scenario with a round-robin event, a fixed host whose date override restricts availability, a loose host, and an existing booking during the override.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time and not round-tripped as a datetime

The `queued` field uses `timezone.now()` as a dataclass default, which Python evaluates once at module import, so every `AssignmentSource` constructed without an explicit value shares the process-start timestamp rather than recording when the source was queued. Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched away

This makes `test_basic` flaky: `(msg,) = messages` can fail with an empty list. The wait should use an un-patched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep as real_sleep` or poll until `messages` is populated), not the patched `time.sleep`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched away

The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), which replaces the global `time.sleep`. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 (and `join()`'s internal sleeps) therefore return immediately and do not actually give the background flusher thread any time to produce. The comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change' is false, so the test still races `step.join()` (which sets `stopped=True`, causing the flusher loop to exit without flushing) against the flusher thread. This makes `test_basic` flaky: `(msg,) = messages` can fail with an empty list. The wait should use an un-patched sleep (e.g. `from time import sleep as real_sleep` or poll until `messages` is populated), not the patched `time.sleep`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring claims one process per shard but default is a single shared process

The class docstring now says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' The implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and round-robins shards across them (`i % num_processes`). Moreover, the `--flusher-processes` click option defaults to 1, so with default configuration a single process handles all shards (the original behavior). The docstring misrepresents both the sharding scheme and the default; it should say that shards are distributed across up to `max_processes` flusher processes and that the default is one process for all shards.

Hung thread workers are never stopped and get duplicated on restart

`_ensure_processes_alive` only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. In the `produce_to_pipe` code path (used by tests), workers are `threading.Thread` instances, so a thread flagged as hung (healthy_since exceeded `spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds`) is never stopped. `_create_process_for_shards` is then called for the same shards, creating a second thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer`. Two flusher threads then concurrently call `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` on the same shards, producing duplicate segment messages and racing on segment acks. Thread mode should either be excluded from the health-restart logic or the old thread must be cooperatively stopped before spawning a replacement.

`_create_process_for_shard` is dead code

The newly added `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` method (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Leaving unused code adds maintenance burden and suggests a shard-level restart path that does not exist. It should be removed (or wired up) before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked completed and committed

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, complete_offset is called in a finally block, so it runs even when result_processor raises. The exception is logged and swallowed, and the commit thread then treats the offset as successfully processed and commits it. A transient processing failure therefore loses the message instead of retrying it; the new error-handling test also expects the offset not to be committed after a processing failure.

OffsetTracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After marking offset 100 committed, all_offsets is pruned and if the remaining set is {102, 103}, start becomes 102, so the method returns 103 and commits offset 104 even though offset 101 was never added or processed. This contradicts the class's stated guarantee and the new gap test; once the first commit occurs, a missing prior offset is no longer treated as blocking.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each queue is created with queue.Queue() without a maxsize, and submit always enqueues immediately. If one group or worker is slow, the consumer continues pulling Kafka messages into memory without limit. The documented 'natural backpressure when queues fill up' never happens, and a slow group can cause unbounded memory growth or an OOM.

Shutdown does not drain queued work

shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Because the worker checks that flag at the top of its loop, it exits after at most the current item and leaves any remaining queued items unprocessed, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incomplete and leaves pending offsets uncommitted.

Submit exceptions are converted into successful offsets

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing, then calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. That marks the message as processed even though no work item was queued, so the offset is committed and the message is dropped. Failures should propagate or be routed to a DLQ rather than being completed.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. On the older Python versions supported by this repository, q.shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), leaving workers blocked in Queue.get() and making the join timeouts ineffective. Additionally, when a worker catches a processing exception, evaluating the except queue.ShutDown clause raises AttributeError and kills the worker thread.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied check now performs a full DB permission query

When the cached permission map is present but does not contain the requested resource, `checkPermission` returns false and Check falls through to `s.getIdentityPermissions` (service.go:139). Since the cache read inside `getUserPermissions` was removed, this path always executes a full DB query (user identifiers, basic role, teams, permissions). The only thing that prevents a DB query on a repeat denied check is the per-resource denial cache. Consequence: the first check for each distinct resource a user cannot access now hits the DB, whereas previously the cached permission map short-circuited it. For denial-heavy traffic or checks over many inaccessible resources, this is a substantial increase in DB load. Consider recording that a cached permission set is known-complete/current so genuine denials can be served without a DB round-trip.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial-cache key can collide across distinct resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example (action="a", name="b_c", parent="d") and (action="a_b", name="c", parent="d") both produce `...perm_<uid>_a_b_c_d`. Folder/dashboard UIDs and parent UIDs can contain underscores, so two distinct resources can map to the same denial key. Consequence: a denial cached for one resource is then served for a different resource the user may be allowed to access (up to the TTL). Use an unescapable delimiter or length-prefix/hash the components.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is never invalidated and can re-deny newly granted (e.g. newly created) resources for 30s

The new permission-denial cache is written whenever a full DB re-query returns not-allowed (service.go:154) and is consulted at the top of Check (service.go:117) to short-circuit to `Allowed:false` without any re-validation. No code path ever deletes these keys on permission changes; they only expire via `shortCacheTTL` (30s). Consequence: once a check is denied, a subsequent grant (including the exact "creator of a just-created dashboard/folder" scenario this PR targets, e.g. a check that runs before the grant is committed) keeps returning `Allowed:false` for up to 30s, reintroducing the bug the PR is meant to fix. Also, because the cache hit is decided by key presence rather than the stored value, any future code that stores `false` under this key would still deny. Consider invalidating denial keys on permission writes (or making this cache consistent with the freshness guarantee of the allow path).

List has no DB fallback for a stale permission map, so newly created resources are omitted

`List` only re-queries the DB when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error, i.e. when the entire per-action permission map is absent. When the map is present but stale, `List` builds its response purely from that cached map, so scopes for dashboards/folders created after the map was cached are omitted for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s). If the reported issue is observed through listing (new resource not appearing right after creation), this path remains unfixed: only `Check` received the DB fallback on a cache miss. Consider applying the same freshness handling to `List`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing React `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in the rule list map

In the `switch (origin)` inside `rules.map(...)` the `grafana` branch renders `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` without a `key`, even though the loop destructures `key` from `ruleWithOrigin` and the `datasource`/`default` branches both pass `key={key}`. This triggers the React "each child in a list should have a unique key" warning and forces index-based reconciliation for these rows, whose children (`RuleActionsButtons`) hold per-row state (silence drawer, clone redirect). It should pass `key={key}` like the other branches.

false_negatives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable after delegating to useAllRulerRuleAbilities

Before this change `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` from the `CombinedRule` group and used it to mark federated rule groups as immutable (no Edit/Delete/Pause). The new implementation delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` (line 245, with a `// TODO: Add support for federated rules` comment) because a `RulerRuleDTO` alone does not carry the group's `source_tenants`. Any component still consuming `useAlertRuleAbility`/`useAlertRuleAbilities` (e.g. RuleDetails) will therefore show Edit/Delete/Pause affordances for federated Mimir rule groups, which are read-only, leading to actions that the backend rejects. The federation check needs to be preserved (pass the group or the federated flag through to the ruler-abilities hook).

Pause and Delete actions never render when the menu is used with promRule only (list view)

The PR makes `AlertRuleMenu` usable with only a `promRule` from the new list view, and adds `grafanaPauseAbility`/`grafanaDeleteAbility` so `canPause`/`canDelete` can become true in that case. However both menu items are still gated on a `rulerRule`: the pause item at line 123 requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and the delete item at line 165 requires `rulerRule && ...`. The new list components (`GrafanaGroupLoader` and `FilterView`) render `GrafanaRuleListItem` -> `RuleActionsButtons.V2` with only `promRule` and never pass a `rulerRule`, so `rulerRule` is always undefined there. As a result, in the new (prom-only) list view the user can no longer Pause or Delete a rule even when the computed `canPause`/`canDelete` (from the Grafana prom abilities) are true and `handleDelete` is wired up. The `canPause`/`canDelete` computations and `handleDelete` prop are effectively dead in that view. Either drop the `rulerRule` guards (the delete handler and `MenuItemPauseRule` should use the prom rule / identifier) or stop computing those abilities for prom-only consumers.

Stale comment/variable name referencing ruler preloading that was removed

The ruler `prefetch` call was removed from `getGroupsAndProvideCache`, but the surrounding comment still says "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX" and the local variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`. Since only Prometheus groups are cached now, the comment and name are misleading about what the code does and should be updated to reflect that only the Prometheus group cache is being warmed.

View link no longer carries returnTo, breaking back-navigation from the rule view

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader`'s `GrafanaRuleListItem` built the view URL with `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new `GrafanaRuleListItem` builds it as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` with no `returnTo`, so navigating from the list into a rule and pressing the "back" control in the rule viewer will no longer return the user to the list/filter they came from. This is a behavior regression from the previous implementation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range guard is evaluated after interpolation

runSplitQuery now interpolates each target before calling `partition(...)`/`querySupportsSplitting`, but `querySupportsSplitting` relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to keep `$__range` queries out of time splitting. Once `applyTemplateVariables` has run, `$__range` has already been substituted (with the full request range), so the check no longer sees the placeholder and those queries are split anyway. The code’s own comment states these queries must not be split because each split uses a different time range; replacing the variable once at the start and then splitting can therefore produce incorrect results. The predicate should be evaluated against the original target expression before interpolation (or the raw flag should be carried through), with a regression test for a `$__range` query.

Targets are interpolated twice in shard splitting

runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target here, then `splitQueriesByStreamShard` calls `runSplitQuery`, which now also interpolates all targets. The shard test was updated to expect `applyTemplateVariables` to be called 5 times for a single original target, confirming the double pass. Template interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent: variable values containing `$`/variable syntax can be expanded a second time, and any non-idempotent rewriting is applied twice after the shard selector has already been injected. Interpolation should happen at one entry point only: either pass already-interpolated targets to a non-interpolating `runSplitQuery` variant, or move interpolation up so shard splitting does not pre-interpolate before calling it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger, discarding recorded log calls

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()` instead of the receiver, so anything logged through `FromContext` is recorded on a discarded logger and is invisible to a test holding the original `*TestLogger`. Because `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` was changed to `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info("Plugin Request Completed", ...)`, a test that injects a `*TestLogger` and asserts on `logger.InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message` will now observe zero calls, and the middleware's log output can no longer be asserted on the injected logger at all. The fake should return the receiver (or share the `Logs` state) so callers can inspect what was logged; otherwise this double silently hides regressions in the newly refactored logging path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the Logger interface is a breaking change for implementers

Adding the `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method to the exported `plugins/log.Logger` interface breaks every implementation. This PR only updates `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger`. Verify there are no other implementations (in particular generated mocks, e.g. via mockery, or test doubles in other packages) that now fail to satisfy the interface and break the build; if any exist they must be regenerated/updated in this PR.

FromContext fallback silently drops traceID and all contextual attributes

`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` type-asserts `d.l.FromContext(ctx)` to `*log.ConcreteLogger` and, on failure, returns `d.New()`. `d.New()` is a base logger with no traceID and no contextual attributes, so if the infra logger ever returns a different implementation (e.g. a context-aware wrapper type), every request-completed log emitted via `LoggerMiddleware` would silently lose pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID with no error or fallback signal. The fallback masks the failure rather than degrading gracefully. Storing the infra `log.Logger` interface (which exposes Debug/Info/etc.) instead of `*log.ConcreteLogger` would avoid the assertion entirely.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and infra FromContext have no tests

The entire refactor now depends on the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`/`instrumentContext` to reproduce the log fields that `LoggerMiddleware` used to add explicitly (endpoint, pluginId, and the conditional dsName/dsUID when `DataSourceInstanceSettings` is set and uname when `User` is set), plus the new `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` in pkg/plugins/log/logger.go (including its `*log.ConcreteLogger` type assertion and `!ok` fallback). None of these are covered by tests; the only test change in the PR is a one-line rename in metrics_middleware_test.go. A regression here (e.g. attributes not being applied or the type assertion failing) would silently drop pluginId/endpoint/uname/dsName/dsUID/traceID from the "Plugin Request Completed" log without any failing test. Add tests asserting the produced contextual attributes.

Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename

The file and middleware were renamed from Instrumentation to Metrics, but the test function is still `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`. This is a leftover from an incomplete rename and is misleading now that `InstrumentationMiddleware` no longer exists. Rename it to `TestMetricsMiddleware` for consistency.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

The limit is enforced with a non-atomic check-then-act: `CountDevices` runs at line 110 and the INSERT/UPSERT runs later at line 120+ without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from different new devices can all read `count < deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the configured limit can be exceeded. The local cache only deduplicates the same device ID and does not prevent this. Use an atomic insert conditioned on the current count, a transaction with appropriate locking, or another mechanism that makes the count and insert serialization atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero affected rows is incorrectly always treated as device limit reached

`updateDevice` treats `RowsAffected() == 0` as `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but zero affected rows does not only mean the device is missing. MySQL by default reports changed rows, not matched rows, so an UPDATE that leaves `client_ip`, `user_agent`, and `updated_at` unchanged can return 0 even though the device exists and is within the limit. This can happen with coarse timestamp precision or with multiple Grafana instances whose local caches are independent. The result is that a legitimate existing device is incorrectly rejected as over the limit. Distinguish 'device not found/stale' from 'matched but unchanged' by checking existence or using found-rows semantics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Failed device-limit write leaves a positive cache entry, allowing retry bypass

In `tagDeviceUI`, the local cache entry is written before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs. If `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, `TagDevice` now returns the error and the unauthenticated request is rejected, but the cache entry remains. The next request from the same device hits the cache check and returns nil without touching the database, so `Anonymous.Authenticate` succeeds even though the device was never stored and the limit is still reached. A user can bypass the new device limit by retrying the request. Set the cache only after a successful write, or delete the key on error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Normal cleanup progress is logged with Error and full ID lists

The cleanup path logs expected normal progress with r.log.Error and includes the entire ids slice. These calls occur for every batch at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579, so a successful cleanup can emit large error-level log entries containing up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs. Combined with the one-minute cleanup ticker this can flood error logs and add significant I/O. Use debug/info level and avoid dumping full ID lists, and do not include the fetch error in a success-path log message.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run now ticks every minute instead of every 10 minutes, so every cleanup job in the slice (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, query history, short URLs, temp files, etc.) runs ten times more often. This is an unrelated global scheduling change not described by the PR and increases database and logging load across the application. Restore the 10-minute interval unless the frequency change is intentional and validated.

false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained under concurrent deletes

The MaxCount cleanup is split into a SELECT that loads excess IDs at OFFSET MaxCount and a later DELETE by those IDs, with no transaction between them. If newer annotations are deleted in that window, rows selected as excess can become part of the newest MaxCount annotations but are still deleted. For example, with MaxCount=1 and annotations id=1 and id=2, cleanup selects id=1 as excess; if a user deletes id=2 before the DELETE runs, cleanup deletes id=1 and leaves zero annotations even though one should have been retained. The PR comment only acknowledges under-deletion from concurrent inserts, not this over-deletion/data-loss case from concurrent deletes.

SQLite parameter-limit test does not actually exceed the modern limit

The new test creates 40003 annotations but splits them across alert, dashboard and API annotation types, so each per-type cleanup batch fetches at most about 13335 IDs. The configured batch size is 32767, but the actual DELETE statement never contains more than about 13335 IDs. On SQLite >= 3.32.0 the variable limit is 32766, so this test would still pass even if deleteByIDs used placeholders instead of inlining the IDs. It therefore does not exercise the >32767-ID case named by the test; create more than 32767 annotations of a single type or test deleteByIDs directly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mode 3 records several metrics with the wrong recorder or arguments

On Storage.Create failure, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration, so unified-storage failures are reported as legacy failures and no storage failure metric is emitted. Update has the same bug at line 129. Delete at line 106 passes the object name as the kind label, producing incorrect and potentially high-cardinality kind values. DeleteCollection at line 166 records the legacy goroutine's result with recordStorageDuration, double-counting storage metrics. These make the dual-writer metrics unreliable for diagnosing mode-3 behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy write failures are silently dropped

The async Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines only feed legacy errors into a metric; no log is emitted. If legacy writes fail because of context cancellation, validation, conflicts, or storage errors, operators get no explicit indication that unified and legacy storage have diverged. At least log the error with kind/name and the fact that it occurred on the async legacy path.

Async legacy writes are unordered and can overwrite newer state

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no sequencing. Two successive updates to the same object can reach legacy storage out of order, and an update can run before the create that preceded it. Legacy storage can therefore end up with older data than unified storage even when both operations succeed, which defeats the purpose of the safety copy. This needs ordered delivery (for example a per-object or per-resource queue) or a different fallback strategy.

Async legacy writes inherit request context and are canceled when the request ends

Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection start legacy writes in goroutines using the handler's request context. Go's HTTP server cancels that context as soon as ServeHTTP returns, so these goroutines will frequently begin with an already-canceled context and the legacy write will fail immediately. The 10-second timeout added inside the goroutine does not help because its parent is already canceled. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (to preserve values such as user/tenant) or a writer-scoped background context before spawning the goroutine.

Delete and DeleteCollection tests spawn async legacy calls that are neither mocked nor awaited

TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection only configure storage expectations. On success, mode 3 launches a goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Delete or d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but the legacy mock has no matching expectation and the test does not wait for the goroutine. That leads to a panic from testify's mock (often asynchronously) and the assertions do not verify that the legacy write happened at all. The tests need legacy mock expectations plus a synchronization mechanism (or an injectable executor) for the async operation.

Legacy update recomputes the update from the legacy object instead of using the stored result

Storage.Update computes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the unified-storage old object. The async legacy path then passes the original objInfo again, so Legacy.Update calls UpdatedObject against the legacy store's old object. For patches/applies or any UpdatedObjectInfo that depends on the current object, the two stores can produce different results and diverge. The previous implementation explicitly wrapped objInfo with the object returned from unified storage; this path should pass a wrapper carrying the storage result (res) instead of the raw objInfo.

Mode 3 Create error test mocks legacy instead of unified storage

The error case for TestMode3_Create configures setupLegacyFn to return an error, but mode 3 calls Storage.Create first. There is no expectation set for the storage mock, so the test will panic on an unexpected mock call instead of exercising the intended storage-error path. This case needs setupStorageFn returning the error (and should leave legacy unconfigured because it should not be called).

Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy propagation

The new mode-3 cases run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which creates/updates via the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists or gets the same data through the legacy API and requires exact equality. Mode 3 intentionally writes to legacy asynchronously, so legacy may not have caught up yet and the test will be flaky or fail. These checks need eventual-consistency polling or should not assert immediate legacy visibility for mode 3.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests each re-read the manifest

GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. On a cold cache under load this means N sequential disk reads/JSON decodes instead of one, and each request's latency is multiplied by the number of queued callers because the lock is held for the entire IO. The standard fix is to re-check the shared state under the write lock (and return it if already populated) before doing the work, or to only compute outside the lock and swap under it, so exactly one goroutine populates the cache.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
In Dev mode every request holds the exclusive write lock during file IO, serializing all callers

When `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` the early return at line 45 is skipped, so every call now takes the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds it for the whole `os.Open` + JSON decode (and potentially the HTTP round-trip to the CDN if the `cdn` branch is ever enabled). Previously concurrent dev requests read the manifest in parallel. Since dev mode intentionally re-reads on every request, a page load issuing several asset requests will now serialize them on this mutex, and a slow/failed read stalls all other callers. If the intent is to always refresh in dev, read/build the result before taking the lock and only swap the pointer (and/or use singleflight to collapse concurrent refresh work) so the critical section contains only the assignment rather than blocking IO.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches. As a result, the SQL expression kill switch always rejects `QueryTypeSQL`, even when the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle is enabled. That leaves the documented feature flag dead and causes users who enable it to still get the internal-looking error `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. If the intent is a permanent hard disable, the flag check should be removed and the documentation/message updated; otherwise this function should return the actual flag value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

A regression test should assert that `QueryTypeSQL` is rejected both when `FlagSqlExpressions` is disabled and when it is enabled, otherwise a future change to `enableSqlExpressions` or the SQL stubs could silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the build lock allows concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu for the duration of the build. getOrCreateIndex performs an unlocked check-then-build, so two callers can both see no index for the same NamespacedResource and enter BuildIndex concurrently. For file-backed indexes both calls use the same directory and call bleve.New on it at the same time; for memory indexes the later `b.cache[key] = idx` overwrites the first. This can cause index creation failures/corruption and can drop watch updates applied to the overwritten index. Add a per-key lock/singleflight, or re-check and serialize index creation for the same key before creating the bleve index.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New TotalDocs log races with index cache writes

The newly added log calls s.search.TotalDocs() after the watch goroutine at lines 207-213 has already been started. bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache without taking cacheMu, while handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex can write b.cache under cacheMu. This is a data race and can panic at startup with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. Either make TotalDocs lock cacheMu or evaluate total docs before starting the watcher.

false_positives.candidate:
Postgres coverage removed from storage-server startup test

The test now unconditionally skips Postgres, removing coverage for a production database at exactly the startup path changed by this PR (resource server initialization moved into the constructor). Because the skip is global rather than CI-specific, a Postgres-specific regression in startup initialization will not be caught. Fix the underlying Postgres issue or scope any temporary skip to CI only.

Shared err and counter are mutated by concurrent init goroutines

Inside searchSupport.init, every errgroup goroutine assigns to the captured outer err variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and returns that same variable, and they also increment totalBatchesIndexed concurrently. These are data races. In particular, another goroutine can overwrite err with nil just before a failing goroutine returns it, so group.Wait can miss a build failure and startup proceeds with a partially built index. Use per-goroutine local errors (or return s.build(...) directly) and an atomic/collected counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup removes hardcoded alias "alias" instead of the created IDPs

The literal "alias" matches no created provider, so none of the 20+ IDPs are actually deleted and the cleanup issues DELETE requests against a non-existent provider. Consequences: if the realm is not fully reset between tests (or cleanup is strict about 404s) this leaks enabled/public IDPs into the realm and can break the count assertions of later tests in the class (e.g. the `getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL, orgaId)` sizes), and at minimum produces useless/erroneous cleanup calls. The same wrong-alias pattern is repeated at line 425 (and the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg line 303). Fix by capturing the created alias in the loop and removing that, e.g. `String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; ... getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias)::remove);`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
New login cache test does not cover unlinking/removing organization brokers or deleting an organization

testCacheIDPForLogin exercises create/update/remove of IDPs and adding a broker to an organization, but never removes a broker from an organization nor deletes an organization. These org-level mutations are exactly the paths that can change which providers appear in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL login lists, and the cache is only refreshed if those operations route through IdentityProviderStorageProvider.update()/remove() and register the login-cache invalidation. Without a test asserting that unlinking a broker (organizationId goes non-null -> null) and deleting an organization clear the login caches and update the returned list, a regression in that invalidation (e.g. an org mutation that bypasses the storage provider, leaving deleted/unlinked providers cached) would go unnoticed. Add assertions that the login caches are cleared and the resulting lists are correct after `organizations().get(orgId).identityProviders().removeIdentityProvider(alias)` / organization removal.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JVM default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` is documented by the `CryptoProvider` interface as returning the (non-FIPS or FIPS) BouncyCastle security provider, but this implementation returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which on a stock JVM is the platform provider (e.g. `SUN`). Any caller that relies on the contract — for example code that registers it as the BC provider or uses BouncyCastle-specific behavior — will receive the wrong provider and fail or silently behave differently. If the intent is to have no BC dependency, the method should either be documented/typed accordingly or the provider should be obtained in a way consistent with the contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence silently returns an empty list for indefinite-length encoding

`readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but `readSequence()` uses that value directly in `while (length > 0)`, so an indefinite-length sequence produces an empty list instead of a clear error. A caller that reads it (e.g. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`) then fails later with the misleading message "Invalid sequence with size different to 2". Since only DER (definite length) is valid here, reject `length == -1` with an explicit error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks external CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI discovered via ServiceLoader. Adding the abstract method `int order()` (without a body) is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every implementation that lives outside this PR. Any existing implementation (e.g. the copy in the keycloak-client repository that this PR says will be synced later, or a third-party provider jar) that was compiled against the previous interface has no `order()` method, so `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` will now throw `AbstractMethodError` when it calls `CryptoProvider::order` on it; recompiling such a provider also fails until it is changed. Providing a `default int order() { return 100; }` would preserve compatibility and let new providers opt into a higher precedence only when needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA test only round-trips conversions and uses a default P-256 key for ES384/ES512

The test generates a single default `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` key (typically P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. It never checks that the reconstructed DER signature actually verifies against the public key, nor that the code handles a curve whose field size matches the algorithm's `getSignatureLength()`. Because `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`/`concatenatedRSToASN1DER` symmetric padding makes the DER→RS→DER→RS round-trip succeed even when `signLength` (66 for ES512) does not match the real 32-byte r/s, the test would pass even if the conversion were wrong for real P-384/P-521 keys. Use a curve matching each algorithm and assert the round-tripped/re-encoded signature verifies against the public key.

Removing the multiple-providers fail-fast allows silent non-deterministic (possibly non-FIPS) selection

Previously `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, forcing an explicit single-provider configuration. The new code only logs the others at debug level and returns `foundProviders.get(0)`. This is dangerous because `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so they tie. The `reversed()` sort is stable, so the winner among tied providers is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath order, which is non-deterministic. A misconfigured FIPS or Elytron deployment that accidentally has both the FIPS/Elytron provider and the default BC provider present would previously fail fast; now it may silently pick the non-FIPS `DefaultCryptoProvider` and run with non-FIPS crypto (or pick the wrong provider on EAP). Consider keeping a hard error when multiple providers share the top order, or at minimum logging at warn/error.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
UnsupportedOperationException thrown from authorization paths that are actually invoked

setPermissionsEnabled()/isPermissionsEnabled() and canExchangeTo() throw UnsupportedOperationException instead of returning false/no-op. These are reachable: AdminPermissions.registerListener() calls clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on ClientRemovedEvent (and roles()/groups() equivalents) whenever Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled; since V1 is enabled by default and can be on together with V2, deleting a client/role/group in a V2 realm will raise UnsupportedOperationException and abort the deletion. Conversely, when only V2 is enabled the listener is skipped entirely, so no cleanup of the deleted entity's resource/policies occurs. canExchangeTo() is invoked by the token-exchange authorization flow and will surface as HTTP 500 rather than a proper denial. These methods should return false/no-op (or be implemented), and the listener guard/cleanup should handle V2.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission cannot find per-client resources

getClientsWithPermission() iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...). However, the per-client resources built by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() are created via resourceStore.create(...) and never get their type set to 'Clients' (only the 'all-clients' resource created in init() has that type and its name is 'Clients'). Consequently per-client grants are never returned; at best the single all-clients resource is evaluated and its name 'Clients' (not a client id) is added to the result. Any caller that uses this method to filter/return the clients an admin can act on receives wrong data. The fix is either to set the resource type when creating per-client resources, or to iterate the actual client resources and evaluate each.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upgraded realms never receive the new Clients resource type and scopes

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already non-null. A realm that had FGAP V2 enabled before this change already has that client, but its resource server only contains the Users resource/scopes; after upgrading, the 'Clients' resource and the configure/map-roles-client-scope/map-roles-composite scopes are never created. As a result, creating a client permission fails in getScope() with ModelValidationException("Scope [configure] does not exist."), getOrCreateResource() for a client throws ModelException("No scopes found."), and ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission() dereferences the null Resource returned by getResourceTypeResource() when calling policyStore.findByResource(server, null). init() must reconcile and add missing resource types/scopes instead of returning when the client exists.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
V2 client role-mapping checks ignore the manage-clients realm role and manage scope

canMapRoles(), canMapCompositeRoles() and canMapClientScopeRoles() only evaluate the fine-grained MAP_ROLES / MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE permissions. Unlike every other method in this class (canManage, canManageClientScopes, canView, canConfigure), they never check root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) nor canManage(client). An administrator holding only the built-in manage-clients role (the normal case, no fine-grained permissions) will therefore be denied adding/removing client roles and composites once V2 is enabled, which is a functional regression versus V1 and is inconsistent with the manage-implies-configure/view behavior implemented in this same class. These methods must also honor the built-in role and/or the manage scope.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Caution says the operator fails without rolling-updates, contradicting the default-strategy test

The new [CAUTION] states the feature rolling-updates must be enabled or the Operator will fail. But UpgradeTest#createInitialDeployment returns without enabling the feature whenever updateStrategy is null (the default '<not set>' strategy), and both testImageChange and testCacheMaxCount expect that default deployment to succeed (recreate on image change, rolling on config change). So the operator demonstrably does not fail in the default case. The caution should be scoped to using the new update.strategy field rather than implying every deployment needs the preview feature, otherwise operators are misled into enabling a preview flag unnecessarily.

New exit code 4 and renumbered exit code 3 are never asserted

testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the printed error string and does not assert that the command exits with FEATURE_DISABLED (4). Likewise testWrongVersions only asserts the error message and never checks the recreate exit code, which this PR just changed from 4 to 3. Since the documented contract is that consumers rely only on the exit code, the two values that matter most for automation are untested; a regression in either the feature-disabled path or the recreate path (e.g. a wrong picocli.exit value) would not be caught.

Renumbering RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE from 4 to 3 breaks the documented exit-code contract

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE was 4 and is now changed to 3, while 4 is reused for the new FEATURE_DISABLED constant. The user guide (and this PR's own docs) explicitly instructs automation to rely solely on the command's exit code, so any pipeline or external caller that treated exit code 4 as 'recreate required' will now receive 3 for that case and 4 for 'feature disabled' — a silent behavioural break. Introducing FEATURE_DISABLED as a new value (e.g. 5) and leaving recreate at 4 would have preserved the contract. Also verify that all internal consumers reference the constant rather than a hard-coded 4, since a literal would now be misinterpreted.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() grants manage with only view permission

The no-argument canManage() returns true when the caller has either VIEW or MANAGE on the all-groups resource: it calls hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE). As a result a principal that only has the `view` scope passes requireManage(), which is invoked by GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup() before creating a top-level group. That lets a view-only administrator create/modify realm group structure, a privilege escalation. The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires only MANAGE, and manage should imply view but not the reverse. The VIEW branch here should be removed (and the interface Javadoc for canManage() that documents VIEW-or-MANAGE is likewise wrong).

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission returns resource ids, not group ids

The findByType callback receives a Resource and uses groupResource.getId() both for the permission lookup (hasPermission(...) internally does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)) and for the returned granted set. Per-group resources are named with the group id (AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource sets name = group.getId()); getId() is the generated Resource UUID, not the group id. So hasPermission() looks up a resource named after a UUID, fails to find it, and silently falls back to the all-groups resource, while the set returned to callers contains resource UUIDs. Callers UsersResource.searchForUser()/getUsersCount() put this set into UserModel.GROUPS to filter users, so users visible only via a group permission are omitted from search/count, and an all-groups VIEW_MEMBERS permission injects a bogus id into the filter. It should use groupResource.getName().

false_positives.candidate:
Per-object resources created by getOrCreateResource never get their type set

getOrCreateResource creates the per-user/per-group Resource via resourceStore.create(...) and updates its scopes but never calls resource.setType(resourceType); only the type-level resources created in init() (e.g. "Groups") get a type. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission relies on resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) to enumerate per-group resources. Because per-group resources are created without a type, findByType only finds the single "Groups" type-level resource, so per-group view-members/manage-members permissions are never seen and group-based user filtering cannot work. The created resource should have resource.setType(resourceType).

requireManageMembers Javadoc references the wrong method

The Javadoc on requireManageMembers(GroupModel) states it throws when {@link #canManageMembership(GroupModel)} is false, but the implementation delegates to canManageMembers(GroupModel). The link is wrong and will mislead maintainers into thinking a different permission is checked; it should reference canManageMembers.

Admin UI message switched from i18next placeholders to Java MessageFormat

The admin UI message bundle uses double-brace interpolation (e.g. {{0}}) throughout, but error-invalid-multivalued-size was changed to single-brace Java MessageFormat placeholders plus a ChoiceFormat expression. Lithuanian login messages replaced with Italian text

No positive test for allowed HTML or matching anchors All four tests only assert that an error is reported for bad fixtures. There is no fixture where valid HTML (for example when English contains , or
) or a matching anchor is expected to produce no message. A regression that rejects every translation containing HTML or anchors would still pass this test suite.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId does not actually verify the encoded grant shortcut

The new matcher checks `items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)` and returns false when it matches. There are two defects: the grant shortcut occupies zero-based positions 4-5 (`substring(4, 6)`), not 3-4, and the condition is inverted. Consequently any access token id with a colon and a UUID suffix passes the matcher regardless of the encoded grant type, so the updated integration tests cannot catch wrong grant-type encoding. It should reject when the prefix length is not 6 or when `substring(4, 6)` is not equal to the expected shortcut.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
