`encodeTokenId` concatenates the grant shortcut directly, while `getTokenContextFromTokenId` requires exactly 6 characters before the colon (lines 74-81). The new `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory#getShortcut()` contract does not require a two-character shortcut, and its Javadoc even says shortcuts are "usually like 3-letters". A custom grant returning a 3-character shortcut will make this server issue token ids like `onrtabc:...` that its own parser rejects with `IllegalArgumentException`, so the encoded context cannot be decoded. Validate that every grant shortcut is exactly two characters and contains no `:`, or make the parser length-aware.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

false_positives.candidate:
setFormParams leaves the cached grantType stale

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked completed and committed

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, complete_offset is called in a finally block, so it runs even when result_processor raises. The exception is logged and swallowed, and the commit thread then treats the offset as successfully processed and commits it. A transient processing failure therefore loses the message instead of retrying it; the new error-handling test also expects the offset not to be committed after a processing failure.

Submit exceptions are converted into successful offsets

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing, then calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. That marks the message as processed even though no work item was queued, so the offset is committed and the message is dropped. Failures should propagate or be routed to a DLQ rather than being completed.

OffsetTracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After marking offset 100 committed, all_offsets is pruned and if the remaining set is {102, 103}, start becomes 102, so the method returns 103 and commits offset 104 even though offset 101 was never added or processed. This contradicts the class's stated guarantee and the new gap test; once the first commit occurs, a missing prior offset is no longer treated as blocking.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. On the older Python versions supported by this repository, q.shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), leaving workers blocked in Queue.get() and making the join timeouts ineffective. Additionally, when a worker catches a processing exception, evaluating the except queue.ShutDown clause raises AttributeError and kills the worker thread.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each queue is created with queue.Queue() without a maxsize, and submit always enqueues immediately. If one group or worker is slow, the consumer continues pulling Kafka messages into memory without limit. The documented 'natural backpressure when queues fill up' never happens, and a slow group can cause unbounded memory growth or an OOM.

Shutdown does not drain queued work

shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Because the worker checks that flag at the top of its loop, it exits after at most the current item and leaves any remaining queued items unprocessed, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incomplete and leaves pending offsets uncommitted.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing span-buf:s keys from sets to sorted sets breaks rolling deployment

The buffer now writes span payloads with zadd and reads/merges them with zcard/zscan/zunionstore, but the Redis key namespace span-buf:s is unchanged while old deployments stored those keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deploy, old and new consumers will operate on the same keys with conflicting types: zadd/zcard/zscan on an existing set and sadd on an existing zset both raise WRONGTYPE. Unflushed segments created before the deploy will therefore fail ingestion/flushing until their TTL expires unless the keys are migrated or the namespace is versioned.

Span-count limit is no longer enforced when loading segments

The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data, and SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans is now unused; eviction is instead hard-coded to 1000 inside the Lua script. If the Python zadd pipeline writes more than 1000 spans and the following EVALSHA calls fail or the process dies between the two pipelines, the set is never evicted. Because the loader no longer rejects oversized segments, such a set can be flushed downstream. The constructor option also no longer controls anything, and its default of 1001 no longer matches the hard-coded 1000 cap.

ZUNIONSTORE default aggregation corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans

The two zunionstore calls use the default SUM aggregation. If the same span payload exists in both the destination set and the set being merged (for example, at-least-once duplicate delivery after a parent merge), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values rather than the actual timestamp. Subsequent zpopmin eviction then treats that duplicate as newer than it really is and may evict newer spans instead. Using AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, depending on the desired tie behavior) would preserve timestamp semantics.

Redirect-chain limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling deep traces

The parent-redirect walk now stops after 1000 iterations, down from 10000. For segment trees deeper than that, set_span_id will remain an intermediate span instead of resolving to the root, so later spans can be placed in the wrong segment. The change is intentional-looking but untested; if the lower bound is desired it should be justified and covered, otherwise it is a silent regression for very deep traces.

No test covers the new eviction cap or duplicate-score behavior

The PR's central behavior is eviction during insert, but every buffer test inserts at most five spans. There is no test that pushes a segment past 1000 spans and asserts that the oldest entries are evicted, no test that verifies max_segment_spans is still honored or intentionally removed, and no test for the zunionstore duplicate-member score behavior. A regression in the cap or in the removed load-time guard would pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Every denied check now performs a full DB permission query

When the cached permission map is present but does not contain the requested resource, `checkPermission` returns false and Check falls through to `s.getIdentityPermissions` (service.go:139). Since the cache read inside `getUserPermissions` was removed, this path always executes a full DB query (user identifiers, basic role, teams, permissions). The only thing that prevents a DB query on a repeat denied check is the per-resource denial cache. Consequence: the first check for each distinct resource a user cannot access now hits the DB, whereas previously the cached permission map short-circuited it. For denial-heavy traffic or checks over many inaccessible resources, this is a substantial increase in DB load. Consider recording that a cached permission set is known-complete/current so genuine denials can be served without a DB round-trip.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying code behavior: when the permission cache is checked, a grant returns immediately, whereas a denial (resource not in cached permission map) ignores the cache and falls through to perform a full database query (`getIdentityPermissions`). Although the golden comment frames the consequence around the security risk of asymmetric cache trust and the candidate frames it around the performance impact of ignoring cached denials, they point to the exact same design flaw in the caching logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial-cache key can collide across distinct resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example (action="a", name="b_c", parent="d") and (action="a_b", name="c", parent="d") both produce `...perm_<uid>_a_b_c_d`. Folder/dashboard UIDs and parent UIDs can contain underscores, so two distinct resources can map to the same denial key. Consequence: a denial cached for one resource is then served for a different resource the user may be allowed to access (up to the TTL). Use an unescapable delimiter or length-prefix/hash the components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys by concatenating components with underscores without escaping, leading to key collisions when components contain underscores, which causes incorrect permission denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is never invalidated and can re-deny newly granted (e.g. newly created) resources for 30s

The new permission-denial cache is written whenever a full DB re-query returns not-allowed (service.go:154) and is consulted at the top of Check (service.go:117) to short-circuit to `Allowed:false` without any re-validation. No code path ever deletes these keys on permission changes; they only expire via `shortCacheTTL` (30s). Consequence: once a check is denied, a subsequent grant (including the exact "creator of a just-created dashboard/folder" scenario this PR targets, e.g. a check that runs before the grant is committed) keeps returning `Allowed:false` for up to 30s, reintroducing the bug the PR is meant to fix. Also, because the cache hit is decided by key presence rather than the stored value, any future code that stores `false` under this key would still deny. Consider invalidating denial keys on permission writes (or making this cache consistent with the freshness guarantee of the allow path).

List has no DB fallback for a stale permission map, so newly created resources are omitted

`List` only re-queries the DB when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error, i.e. when the entire per-action permission map is absent. When the map is present but stale, `List` builds its response purely from that cached map, so scopes for dashboards/folders created after the map was cached are omitted for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s). If the reported issue is observed through listing (new resource not appearing right after creation), this path remains unfixed: only `Check` received the DB fallback on a cache miss. Consider applying the same freshness handling to `List`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests each re-read the manifest

GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. On a cold cache under load this means N sequential disk reads/JSON decodes instead of one, and each request's latency is multiplied by the number of queued callers because the lock is held for the entire IO. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `i.content` can be nil in RSS feeds, which causes `i.content.scrub` to throw an error, and both suggest falling back to `description`.

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged for that mode. `Jobs::PollFeed` feeds `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content)` into this path, so an RSS/Atom item containing encoded markup such as `<script>...</script>` is stored and later rendered with `raw post.cooked`; the script executes in the forum/embed origin. Ruby's `Kernel#open` executes a command when the filename starts with `|`; the Disqus importer passes `t[:link]` from the XML export directly into this method with no scheme validation, so a malicious export can run arbitrary shell commands when the importer is executed. The absolutization only handles paths beginning with `/` by stripping all leading slashes and prefixing the source host. For a protocol-relative URL such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png`, it produces `http://sourcehost/cdn.example.com/image.png` instead of `http://cdn.example.com/image.png`, breaking embedded images and links. postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

For attachments this bypasses `max_attachment_size_kb`: files up to 10 MB are allowed client-side even when the site limit is lower, and files larger than 10 MB are rejected even when the site setting allows them. The loop makes at most five 80% resize attempts, then calls `Upload.create_for` without checking `tempfile.size` again against `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. If five attempts are not enough, the new guard has not actually enforced the limit and the oversized file proceeds to upload. The loop also ignores the boolean result of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, so a failed conversion still consumes an attempt and leaves the original size unchanged. The new call passes `tempfile.path` as the source to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated branch only when the source path matches `/\.GIF$/i`, but Rack multipart temp files normally do not carry the original uploaded extension. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

This has two failure modes: (1) if the user has no working-hours entry for that weekday, find returns undefined and the slot falls through as available, so fixed hosts can be booked on their days off; (2) if the user has multiple ranges on the same weekday, such as 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00, an afternoon slot is compared only against the first range and rejected even though it is within the second range. true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

The containment test rejects a slot only when slotEndTime is before/equal overrideStart or slotStartTime is after overrideEnd. It therefore accepts slots that partially overlap an override: a 13:30-14:30 slot with a 14:00-18:00 override starts before the override but ends inside and is treated as within the override; a slot starting exactly at 18:00 is also accepted because the end check uses strict isAfter. Combined with the early return on dateOverrideExist, these slots bypass normal working hours and busy checks. false_positives.candidate:
Date override path returns true before busy-time checks

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot falls inside a date override the function sets dateOverrideExist and then returns true at line 133 before the busy.every(...) check at line 153. The busy array contains the host's Cal bookings and calendar busy times. As a result, any fixed host with a date override appears free for the whole override even when already booked, so personal and round-robin events can create double bookings on override days. The override should bypass normal working-hour checks only; busy times still need to be evaluated.

Active date overrides are still selected by the override wall-clock UTC date

activeOverrides is selected by comparing dayjs.utc(override.start) directly against the invitee's local day boundaries. Date override start values are stored as wall-clock times (for example, 14:00 Asia/Kolkata is stored as 14:00Z), so this comparison works only when the organizer and invitee dates happen to align. For a large positive invitee offset such as UTC+14, an override stored at 14:00Z on the invitee day falls after the invitee day's UTC end boundary (10:00Z the same day), so the override is filtered out and the new timezone conversion is never applied. The filter should compare the converted instant or otherwise test overlap against the invitee day.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin date override fix

The PR description says fixed-host date overrides in round-robin events are fixed and should prevent bookings when the fixed host is unavailable, but the added test only changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It has no ROUND_ROBIN event, no fixed host with a date override, and no busy booking on the override day. As a result, the regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (busy times being skipped and the working-hours filtering) are not caught. Add a scenario with a round-robin event, a fixed host whose date override restricts availability, a loose host, and an existing booking during the override.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increment is a lost-update race under overlapping cron runs

On failure, both paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read before the network call. The cron endpoint has no lock or claim preventing overlapping invocations. Two runs can process the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio (causing duplicate SMS), and both write the same incremented value. As a result, two failures can leave `retryCount` at 1 instead of 2, so the reminder is retried more often than intended and may never reach the deletion threshold. Use an atomic update such as `{ increment: 1 }` and claim the row (e.g. conditional update or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) before sending.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency/race condition issue where `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` reads a stale value and causes lost updates, and both suggest using Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` across both failure paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS and already-scheduled reminders

The second branch of the cleanup `deleteMany` has only `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`. It is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, so this SMS cron will delete any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1`, including non-SMS reminders if the field is used elsewhere, and including rows that are already marked as scheduled. Deleting a scheduled row drops its provider reference (for example the Twilio SID) while the provider-side message may still be queued, and it can no longer be cancelled through the normal workflow path. Add the method and unscheduled predicates to this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact problem described in the golden comment: the deletion logic (`deleteMany`) has a branch with `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` that lacks the `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, causing it to incorrectly delete non-SMS workflow reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Retry update failure can abort the whole reminder batch

The new `retryCount` update inside the `catch` block is not itself protected. If it fails, for example because another cron invocation already deleted the row or because of a transient database error, the exception escapes the catch, aborts the `for` loop, and prevents every remaining due reminder from being processed. The endpoint then returns 500 instead of continuing with the rest of the batch. Perform this update in its own try/catch or use `updateMany` so one stale row cannot break processing of other reminders.

The `try` block wraps both `twilio.scheduleSMS` and the subsequent database update. If Twilio successfully schedules the SMS but the database update fails, execution enters this catch, increments `retryCount`, and leaves `scheduled` false without persisting `scheduledSMS.sid`. On the next cron run the same reminder is still considered unscheduled and the SMS is sent again, producing a duplicate message to the recipient. This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from `InsightsBookingService` and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The diff updates only this service and its tests; no other call sites are migrated. Any code that invokes `service.findMany({...})` will fail to compile (method no longer exists), and any caller that relied on the previous behavior (merging caller-supplied `where`/`select`/pagination with the authorization and filter conditions) must now build and execute its own `$queryRaw`. The single test that runs the generated SQL (`prisma.$queryRaw ... WHERE ${baseConditions}`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose authorization condition contains no array parameter. The security-critical org/team paths, which build `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})`, are only checked structurally via `toEqual(Prisma.sql...)` and never executed. Prisma array binding into `ANY($1)` has known type-inference pitfalls (e.g. requiring a cast such as `::int[]`, or failing when the array is empty). A broken/empty array binding would therefore pass this suite but throw or silently return no rows in production, which is precisely the parameter-binding risk the PR description flags.

The org-scope test compares the service's `Prisma.Sql` to a literal with `teamIds` ordered `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `userIds` ordered `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. The PR deletes the entire "Caching" describe block (the `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions` tests), but the service still caches results via `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` in `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`. In `requestReschedule`, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are called inside `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` without awaiting. The handler first runs `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` and only afterwards looks up `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Because the cleanup runs first, any cancelled reminder whose `scheduledDate` has just passed is deleted from the DB without ever being cancelled in SendGrid, so the reminder email is delivered. Since this cron runs every 15 minutes, a cancellation made within ~15 minutes of a reminder's send time (after the last cron run while the reminder was still in the future) falls into this gap and the email goes out. The cancellation pass should run before/independent of the past-reminder cleanup, and the window/cadence must guarantee every reminder is cancelled before its send time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use enforcement is a non-atomic read-modify-write

Backup-code consumption is implemented as: decrypt the stored array, set `backupCodes[index] = null`, then `prisma.user.update` with a re-encrypted copy. This is a classic TOCTOU read-modify-write with no locking or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests that present the same backup code can both read the pre-update value, both find the code valid, and both succeed — so a single backup code can be used more than once under concurrency. Since backup codes are a recovery/second-factor credential, being able to replay one defeats the 'used exactly once' guarantee stated in the UI copy. A conditional/atomic update (e.g. compare-and-set on the ciphertext, or a DB transaction with row lock) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same race condition (TOCTOU) where backup codes are decrypted, modified in memory, and written back non-atomically, allowing concurrent login requests to reuse a single-use backup code.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login can bypass password verification when a totpCode is also sent

Password verification is gated on `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), while the backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is truthy (line 131), regardless of whether a `totpCode` was supplied. Because these two conditions are independent, a request that contains a valid backup code AND any non-empty `totpCode` value skips password checking but still goes through the backup-code validation path. The consequence is that anyone holding a single leaked backup code can log in with just that code plus a garbage totpCode, without knowing the account password — the backup code ceases to be a second factor and becomes a single factor. The UI happens to set `totpCode` to an empty string in backup mode, so this is only reachable by calling the credentials provider directly, but it is a real authentication bypass of the password requirement. The backup-code branch should also require the password (or the password check should not be skipped merely because `totpCode` is present when `backupCode` is being used).

Dismissing the dialog after enabling 2FA never calls onEnable, leaving the toggle out of sync

Previously `handleEnable` called `onEnable()` immediately on success. Now it transitions to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is only invoked from the explicit 'Close' button (line 269). The `Dialog`'s `onOpenChange` (line 166) is still wired straight to the parent, so a user who dismisses the modal via Escape, backdrop click, or the close (X) button after the TOTP code was accepted leaves the server-side 2FA enabled (the enable endpoint already set `twoFactorEnabled: true`) while the parent never runs `onEnable()` / refetch, so the settings switch and related state can continue to display 2FA as disabled. The finalization should happen on any close path (or the parent should refetch on close), not only on the dedicated Close button.

No test covers the core feature: logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The PR description's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the added e2e steps only click the download and copy buttons and then close the dialog; both content assertions are left as `// TODO` and nothing exercises the actual backup-code path. The two security-sensitive behaviors this PR introduces — consuming a backup code during login (single-use invalidation) and disabling 2FA via a backup code — have zero automated coverage. Given the password-bypass and single-use race described elsewhere, the absence of a test that actually signs in with a backup code and asserts that the same code is then rejected leaves these regressions undetected. At minimum, a login-with-backup-code test (and the already-flagged 'TODO' file-content check) should be added.

Existing 2FA users have no backup codes and no way to generate them, making 'Lost access' a dead end

`backupCodes` is a new nullable column, so every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has `user.backupCodes === null`. When such a user uses 'Lost access' and submits anything, they hit `if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`, which renders `t("missing_backup_codes")` = 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' That instruction is impossible to follow: the only endpoint that creates backup codes is `setup.ts`, which returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` for users who already have 2FA on, and this PR adds no 'regenerate backup codes' UI. These users are therefore permanently locked out of the recovery path (they must disable and re-enable 2FA, which is exactly what the feature is meant to avoid). Either the message should not tell users to do something the product does not offer, or a way to generate/regenerate backup codes for already-enabled 2FA should be provided.

Exhausting all backup codes reports 'incorrect code' instead of 'no backup codes'

After codes are consumed they are set to `null` but the array (and therefore the encrypted string) is never emptied, so `user.backupCodes` remains a truthy JSON string of nulls. The guard on line 137 (`if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`) never fires once all codes are used; instead `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` returns -1 and the user is told `incorrect_backup_code` forever. A user with zero remaining codes should be told they have none left (the `MissingBackupCodes` path) rather than being told each retry that their code is wrong.

`referencesToCreate` for `updateLocation` now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never puts those fields on its returned EventResult. Editing a booking location therefore creates BookingReference rows with both fields undefined. Previously the `evt.destinationCalendar` fallback populated them. Later updates/cancellations may then target the wrong calendar or fail to find the external event.

Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is explicitly set to `null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. The optional push then silently does nothing, so `teamDestinationCalendars` collected from the other collective hosts is discarded. In that case EventManager never receives those hosts' destination calendars and collective hosts do not get calendar invites. The array should be initialised to `[]` before collecting/pushing team destinations.

Hangout-link patch uses undefined calendarId when destination is absent

`selectedCalendar` can be undefined when no destination calendar matches the credential, and insert correctly falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`. The follow-up `events.patch` still passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, so in the fallback case the patch is sent with an undefined calendar id and the generated hangoutLink is not written into the event description. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` fallback in the patch.

Lark createEvent also ignores credentialId and uses the first destination

The Lark implementation now takes the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` for every credential. For a collective booking, the second host's Lark credential will attempt to use the first host's calendarId, likely failing or writing to the wrong calendar. `createEvent` needs to choose the destination entry matching the credential it was called with.

Base CalDAV service ignores credentialId when selecting destination calendars

With multiple destination calendars, `createEvent` filters the credential's calendars by the first destination's externalId. For the second host's credential that externalId belongs to another account, so the filter produces no calendars and the method returns success without creating anything. The selection must be made using the `credentialId` passed to `createEvent` or another identifier that belongs to the current credential.

Recurring collective cancellation only uses organizer credentials and repeats deletes

When cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, the loop over the new multiple calendar references re-enters the same block for every reference, but inside it ignores the current reference and only iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials`, deleting the first calendar reference of every updated booking. For a collective booking, second-host references/credentials are never used, so those external events remain, and the same organizer deletions are issued once per reference.

No test for collective multi-host destination calendars

The only test change updates the expected webhook shape for BOOKING_REJECTED. There is no test covering collective events with multiple destination calendars or the new create/update/delete paths, despite many calendar services and EventManager being changed. This leaves the primary regression and the calendar-service credential-selection bugs untested.

This PR updates only a small set of call sites, so other consumers will read `.lib`, `.metadata`, or `.credentials` from a Promise and get undefined, breaking calendar, video, and payment integrations at runtime (and likely failing typecheck where the old module type is expected). Either keep a synchronous metadata map or update every consumer and the exported type to the async contract.

Because `getCalendar` became async, `getCalendarCredentials` now stores a `Promise<Calendar | null>` in the `calendar` field while remaining a synchronous function. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await that field. Any other caller of this exported function that treats `calendar` as a Calendar will call methods on a Promise. Make the function async and await `getCalendar`, or explicitly change the return type to expose promises and migrate all callers.

requestReschedule fires calendar deletion asynchronously without awaiting it

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside an async callback that the mutation never awaits. `readLength()` returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but `readSequence()` uses that value directly in `while (length > 0)`, so an indefinite-length sequence produces an empty list instead of a clear error. A caller that reads it (e.g. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`) then fails later with the misleading message "Invalid sequence with size different to 2". Since only DER (definite length) is valid here, reject `length == -1` with an explicit error.

The candidate describes the concrete consequence—skipping the loop and returning an empty list—rather than the golden comment's concern about length arithmetic, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract order() breaks external CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider is a public SPI discovered via ServiceLoader. Adding the abstract method `int order()` (without a body) is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every implementation that lives outside this PR. Any existing implementation (e.g. the copy in the keycloak-client repository that this PR says will be synced later, or a third-party provider jar) that was compiled against the previous interface has no `order()` method, so `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` will now throw `AbstractMethodError` when it calls `CryptoProvider::order` on it; recompiling such a provider also fails until it is changed. Providing a `default int order() { return 100; }` would preserve compatibility and let new providers opt into a higher precedence only when needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations that do not implement it. The candidate elaborates on source and runtime consequences and proposes a default method.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing the multiple-providers fail-fast allows silent non-deterministic (possibly non-FIPS) selection

Previously `detectProvider` threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, forcing an explicit single-provider configuration. The new code only logs the others at debug level and returns `foundProviders.get(0)`. This is dangerous because `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so they tie. The `reversed()` sort is stable, so the winner among tied providers is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath order, which is non-deterministic. A misconfigured FIPS or Elytron deployment that accidentally has both the FIPS/Elytron provider and the default BC provider present would previously fail fast; now it may silently pick the non-FIPS `DefaultCryptoProvider` and run with non-FIPS crypto (or pick the wrong provider on EAP). Consider keeping a hard error when multiple providers share the top order, or at minimum logging at warn/error.

ECDSA test only round-trips conversions and uses a default P-256 key for ES384/ES512

The test generates a single default `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` key (typically P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. It never checks that the reconstructed DER signature actually verifies against the public key, nor that the code handles a curve whose field size matches the algorithm's `getSignatureLength()`. Because `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`/`concatenatedRSToASN1DER` symmetric padding makes the DER→RS→DER→RS round-trip succeed even when `signLength` (66 for ES512) does not match the real 32-byte r/s, the test would pass even if the conversion were wrong for real P-384/P-521 keys. Use a curve matching each algorithm and assert the round-tripped/re-encoded signature verifies against the public key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined or stopped on failure, allowing test hang or false pass

The test starts a non-daemon thread at line 139 and only sets deletedAll after all deletes. There is no try/finally around the deletes and no join after line 155. If any delete throws, the thread loops forever and can hang the test JVM; even on success the assertion at line 157 runs while the reader may still be in flight, so an exception can be added after the assertion and be silently missed, and the thread can keep using the realm after teardown. Use try/finally to stop the loop and join the thread, and coordinate the first read (for example with a latch) so the race is actually exercised.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same race: the reader thread is not joined, so the assertion can run before an in-flight read records an exception, causing a false pass. Its additional failure and teardown concerns do not detract from this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Hung thread workers are never stopped and get duplicated on restart

`_ensure_processes_alive` only calls `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. In the `produce_to_pipe` code path (used by tests), workers are `threading.Thread` instances, so a thread flagged as hung (healthy_since exceeded `spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds`) is never stopped. `_create_process_for_shards` is then called for the same shards, creating a second thread with a fresh `SpansBuffer`. Two flusher threads then concurrently call `flush_segments`/`done_flush_segments` on the same shards, producing duplicate segment messages and racing on segment acks. Thread mode should either be excluded from the health-restart logic or the old thread must be cooperatively stopped before spawning a replacement.

Docstring claims one process per shard but default is a single shared process

The class docstring now says 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing.' The implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and round-robins shards across them (`i % num_processes`). Moreover, the `--flusher-processes` click option defaults to 1, so with default configuration a single process handles all shards (the original behavior). The docstring misrepresents both the sharding scheme and the default; it should say that shards are distributed across up to `max_processes` flusher processes and that the default is one process for all shards.

`_create_process_for_shard` is dead code

The newly added `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` method (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere in the codebase; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts via `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. Leaving unused code adds maintenance burden and suggests a shard-level restart path that does not exist. It should be removed (or wired up) before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

New PR comment helpers are called on the wrong class

60-second deadline can leave an auth identity batch unprocessed

`check_auth` marks `last_synced` for every selected identity before scheduling `check_auth_identities`, and that task processes up to 100 identities sequentially and only reschedules at the end. A 60-second processing deadline can kill the task before it finishes or reaches the reschedule, leaving the remaining identities unprocessed until the next ~24-hour cycle. Increase/remove the deadline, or update/reschedule identities incrementally so a timeout does not silently skip work.

Custom renderer return value is checked by truthiness

`if (cell)` treats valid custom renderer results like `0` or the empty string as “no custom renderer” and falls back to the default renderer. true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset 'advanced' branch passes a negative slice to Django and raises

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset = cursor.offset (negative). Django QuerySets do not support negative slicing; `QuerySet.__getitem__` raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (ValueError in some versions) for a negative slice start. The comment claims 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. A client can craft a cursor like `value:-1:0` (Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets), triggering a 500 for anyone who reaches this code path. The negative-offset feature is therefore non-functional and provides a way to crash the endpoint.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses a negative slice offset on a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative slicing and raises an AssertionError. The candidate adds triggering conditions and impact without changing the underlying issue.

Although it does not specifically mention API-key/org-token authentication or optimized_pagination=true, it points to the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate datetime-keyed querysets used by audit logs

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (line 838-840) and value_from_cursor (842-843) are numeric-only: get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) ...)` on the attribute named by the order_by key, and value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value. The new audit-log endpoint instantiates this paginator with order_by="-datetime", where AuditLogEntry.datetime is a DateTimeField. On the very first page (after fetching rows) `build_cursor` calls `get_item_key(results[-1])`, and `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, producing a 500. Even if that were fixed, value_from_cursor returning an int would be fed into `build_queryset`'s WHERE clause as the datetime value, so subsequent pages would filter incorrectly or error in Postgres. This paginator should extend DateTimePaginator (which formats/parses datetimes) rather than duplicating Paginator's numeric handling. As written, every request that reaches the optimized path crashes.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: get_item_key uses numeric math.floor/ceil on the datetime field when the audit logs paginator uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError. Its additional discussion of cursor parsing does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator 'negative offset' change is a no-op and the comment misdescribes behavior

The new `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` is behavior-identical to the previous `queryset[offset:stop]` for all non-negative offsets, and for is_prev it keeps offset unchanged, so it does not enable 'bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning' as the comment claims. For a negative non-prev offset it only changes behavior by silently clamping to 0 (previously the negative slice errored) rather than improving performance. The comment is misleading about both the purpose and the safety of the change; the underlying Django ORM does not support negative offsets, so they are neither efficient nor safe.

Cursor comment claims negative offsets are allowed but code is unchanged

The added comment says 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios', but `self.offset = int(offset)` is exactly the original line and performs no validation or special handling. Cursor offsets have always been able to be negative (from_string parses arbitrary ints); the comment implies a new capability that does not exist and contradicts the actual negative-offset handling elsewhere. It should be removed or reworded to describe real behavior.

No tests for the new OptimizedCursorPaginator or the optimized endpoint branch

The PR adds a new paginator class and a request-controlled branch in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint (including an authorization check and a negative-offset code path) with no unit or endpoint tests. Given that the datetime-key mismatch and negative-offset crash above would be caught by even a single test exercising optimize_pagination=true on the audit-log endpoint, the absence of tests means these regressions ship undetected. Add tests covering the optimized path with datetime ordering, the permission gate, and crafted negative-offset cursors.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu for the duration of the build. getOrCreateIndex performs an unlocked check-then-build, so two callers can both see no index for the same NamespacedResource and enter BuildIndex concurrently. For file-backed indexes both calls use the same directory and call bleve.New on it at the same time; for memory indexes the later `b.cache[key] = idx` overwrites the first. This can cause index creation failures/corruption and can drop watch updates applied to the overwritten index. Add a per-key lock/singleflight, or re-check and serialize index creation for the same key before creating the bleve index.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu locking to the final cache assignment allows concurrent BuildIndex calls to build duplicate indexes for the same key. The candidate adds consequences and mitigation suggestions without changing the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked completed and committed

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, complete_offset is called in a finally block, so it runs even when result_processor raises. The exception is logged and swallowed, and the commit thread then treats the offset as successfully processed and commits it. A transient processing failure therefore loses the message instead of retrying it; the new error-handling test also expects the offset not to be committed after a processing failure.

Submit exceptions are converted into successful offsets

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing, then calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. That marks the message as processed even though no work item was queued, so the offset is committed and the message is dropped. Failures should propagate or be routed to a DLQ rather than being completed.

OffsetTracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After marking offset 100 committed, all_offsets is pruned and if the remaining set is {102, 103}, start becomes 102, so the method returns 103 and commits offset 104 even though offset 101 was never added or processed. This contradicts the class's stated guarantee and the new gap test; once the first commit occurs, a missing prior offset is no longer treated as blocking.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. On the older Python versions supported by this repository, q.shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), leaving workers blocked in Queue.get() and making the join timeouts ineffective. Additionally, when a worker catches a processing exception, evaluating the except queue.ShutDown clause raises AttributeError and kills the worker thread.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each queue is created with queue.Queue() without a maxsize, and submit always enqueues immediately. If one group or worker is slow, the consumer continues pulling Kafka messages into memory without limit. The documented 'natural backpressure when queues fill up' never happens, and a slow group can cause unbounded memory growth or an OOM.

Shutdown does not drain queued work

shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Because the worker checks that flag at the top of its loop, it exits after at most the current item and leaves any remaining queued items unprocessed, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incomplete and leaves pending offsets uncommitted.

The buffer now writes span payloads with zadd and reads/merges them with zcard/zscan/zunionstore, but the Redis key namespace span-buf:s is unchanged while old deployments stored those keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deploy, old and new consumers will operate on the same keys with conflicting types: zadd/zcard/zscan on an existing set and sadd on an existing zset both raise WRONGTYPE. Unflushed segments created before the deploy will therefore fail ingestion/flushing until their TTL expires unless the keys are migrated or the namespace is versioned.

Span-count limit is no longer enforced when loading segments

The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data, and SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans is now unused; eviction is instead hard-coded to 1000 inside the Lua script. If the Python zadd pipeline writes more than 1000 spans and the following EVALSHA calls fail or the process dies between the two pipelines, the set is never evicted. Because the loader no longer rejects oversized segments, such a set can be flushed downstream. The constructor option also no longer controls anything, and its default of 1001 no longer matches the hard-coded 1000 cap.

ZUNIONSTORE default aggregation corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans

The two zunionstore calls use the default SUM aggregation. If the same span payload exists in both the destination set and the set being merged (for example, at-least-once duplicate delivery after a parent merge), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values rather than the actual timestamp. Subsequent zpopmin eviction then treats that duplicate as newer than it really is and may evict newer spans instead. Using AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, depending on the desired tie behavior) would preserve timestamp semantics.

Redirect-chain limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling deep traces

The parent-redirect walk now stops after 1000 iterations, down from 10000. For segment trees deeper than that, set_span_id will remain an intermediate span instead of resolving to the root, so later spans can be placed in the wrong segment. The change is intentional-looking but untested; if the lower bound is desired it should be justified and covered, otherwise it is a silent regression for very deep traces.

No test covers the new eviction cap or duplicate-score behavior

The PR's central behavior is eviction during insert, but every buffer test inserts at most five spans. There is no test that pushes a segment past 1000 spans and asserts that the oldest entries are evicted, no test that verifies max_segment_spans is still honored or intentionally removed, and no test for the zunionstore duplicate-member score behavior. A regression in the cap or in the removed load-time guard would pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email validation mutates statistics and double-counts failed signups

The validator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which increments `match_count` and saves the record (app/models/blocked_email.rb:14-16). Because `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` at line 168 and then `user.save` at line 172, the same email is validated twice, so one failed signup increments `match_count` twice and updates `last_match_at` twice. Any other `valid?` call also changes the stats. Move the match statistics update out of the validation path (record it in the controller only when the email is actually rejected), or make the validator check read-only. The read-modify-write is also not atomic, so concurrent checks can lose increments.

Removing float: right from .panel loses right alignment in non-flex / legacy-box renderers

`.panel` previously used `float: right;` to sit at the right edge of the header. That rule was removed and replaced by `margin-left: auto;` inside the new flex `.contents` container. Auto margins on flex items are not supported by the 2009 `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` implementations (the reason those prefixed `display` values are emitted by the `flexbox` mixin), and are ignored entirely by browsers with no flex support (e.g. IE9), which is why the prefixed `display` values exist. In those renderers the panel loses its float and now flows immediately after `.title`/`.extra-info-wrapper` instead of being right-aligned, so the header layout degrades exactly in the browsers the mixin is meant to cover. Keep the float as a fallback (floats are inert inside a real flex container) or otherwise provide a fallback.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits a non-existent -ms-align-items declaration and invalid -webkit-box-align values

`-ms-align-items` (line 121) is not a real property — IE10 uses `-ms-flex-align`, which is already emitted — so that line is dead code. More importantly, `-webkit-box-align` (line 118) does not accept the `baseline` value, which is exactly what the new call site in `app/assets/stylesheets/common/components/badges.css.scss:57` passes (`@include align-items(baseline)`). In old WebKit, where this mixin switches the element to `display: -webkit-inline-box`, the declaration is discarded and `-webkit-box-align` falls back to `stretch`, so the bullet badge children can be stretched to the line box instead of baseline-aligned; previously those browsers got the `inline-block` fallback and normal inline alignment. true_positives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

`order` mixin maps order values to -webkit-box-ordinal-group/-moz-box-ordinal-group without the required +1 offset

The 2009 box model properties `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group` are 1-based and must be positive integers, while the modern `order` property is 0-based and also accepts negatives. Passing `$val` straight through means `@include order(1)` emits `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: 1`, which is the default and therefore a no-op, and `@include order(0)` emits an invalid value that old WebKit/Gecko discard. The current call sites (`order(2)`, `order(3)`) happen to keep the correct relative order only because the unordered `.title` implicitly stays at group 1, but the mixin is unsafe for any future use. Emit `$val + 1` for the `*-box-ordinal-group` properties.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: legacy -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group are 1-based, so passing $val directly, especially 0, produces invalid values and can cause layout issues in older browsers.

`include_website_name` is missing the trailing `?` and is never invoked

As a result `website_name` is always serialized, emitting `website_name: null` for every user with no website (and any other case the guard was meant to exclude). false_positives.candidate:
Imported feed content is stored as unsanitized raw HTML

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: raw_html`, and `Post#cook` returns `raw` unchanged for that mode. `Jobs::PollFeed` feeds `CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content)` into this path, so an RSS/Atom item containing encoded markup such as `<script>...</script>` is stored and later rendered with `raw post.cooked`; the script executes in the forum/embed origin. Remote feed content is not trusted; it must be sanitized/allowlisted before being stored as raw HTML, or this path must not use `raw_html`.

Kernel#open on a caller-supplied URL can execute shell commands

`import_remote` calls `open(url).read` on a URL supplied by callers. Ruby's `Kernel#open` executes a command when the filename starts with `|`; the Disqus importer passes `t[:link]` from the XML export directly into this method with no scheme validation, so a malicious export can run arbitrary shell commands when the importer is executed. Validate the URL scheme/host and use a non-command-opening HTTP API, or at least reject pipe and non-http URLs.

Protocol-relative URLs are rewritten to the source host

The absolutization only handles paths beginning with `/` by stripping all leading slashes and prefixing the source host. For a protocol-relative URL such as `//cdn.example.com/image.png`, it produces `http://sourcehost/cdn.example.com/image.png` instead of `http://cdn.example.com/image.png`, breaking embedded images and links. Treat URLs beginning with `//` as protocol-relative and use the source scheme.

PollFeed setting tests short-circuit on feed_polling_enabled

The 'requires feed_polling_url' and 'requires embed_by_username' examples only stub the one setting to nil but leave `feed_polling_enabled?` at its default false, so the first condition short-circuits and `poll_feed` is never called regardless of the setting under test. Duplicate downsize definition silently removes the existing width/height API

Ruby does not support method overloading: defining `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces the earlier `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145. Any existing caller using the old signature, e.g. `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, temp, 100, 100, opts)`, will now raise ArgumentError. A four-positional call passing width and height will be interpreted as width plus opts and fail when the code reads `opts[:allow_animation]`. The old public method is no longer usable, so this needs to be a distinct method name or a single method that accepts both forms.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the later dimensions-string signature overrides the earlier width/height signature, making the original API unreachable and breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hard-coded 10 MB no longer honors configured attachment size limits

`validateUploadedFile` is used for both images and attachments, but the new code replaces `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` with a fixed `10 * 1024` KB. For attachments this bypasses `max_attachment_size_kb`: files up to 10 MB are allowed client-side even when the site limit is lower, and files larger than 10 MB are rejected even when the site setting allows them. The 413 handler at line 246 repeats the same hard-coded assumption and can display the wrong limit.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hard-coded 10 MB limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client/server limit mismatches, and also notes the same incorrect assumption in the 413 handler.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop can proceed with a file still over the limit and ignores failed conversions

The loop makes at most five 80% resize attempts, then calls `Upload.create_for` without checking `tempfile.size` again against `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. If five attempts are not enough, the new guard has not actually enforced the limit and the oversized file proceeds to upload. The loop also ignores the boolean result of `OptimizedImage.downsize`, so a failed conversion still consumes an attempt and leaves the original size unchanged. The code needs a post-loop size check and an explicit abort/error path when conversion fails or the file remains too large.

Animated GIF detection uses the temp path, so uploaded animations can be flattened

The new call passes `tempfile.path` as the source to `OptimizedImage.downsize`. `OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated branch only when the source path matches `/\.GIF$/i`, but Rack multipart temp files normally do not carry the original uploaded extension. As a result, `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is ineffective for normal uploads and animated GIFs are handled by the static `downsize_instructions`, whose `convert ... #{from}[0]` keeps only the first frame. Animated uploads can silently become static images.

Remote URL downloads now ignore configured size limits for all upload types

Changing `FileHelper.download` from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to `10.megabytes` applies to every URL upload, including non-images. A site with a smaller `max_attachment_size_kb` or `max_image_size_kb` will now fetch up to 10 MB from the remote URL before validation, increasing resource use and bypassing the configured limit. If larger images are intended only so they can be auto-downsized, the download limit should be conditional on the upload type or based on an explicit setting.

No tests cover the new auto-downsize path

The PR changes upload size enforcement, overwrites uploaded image files, and relies on method dispatch inside `OptimizedImage`, but adds no tests for oversized static images, animated GIFs, failed conversions, non-image uploads, or the five-attempt cap. Regressions such as the duplicate `downsize` method or the animation branch being skipped would not be caught.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes when the user has no TopicUser row

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (e.g. the link is forwarded/shared, or the user follows `/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe` for a topic they never interacted with, or a notification was generated without creating a TopicUser). The next line `if tu.notification_level > ...` dereferences nil and raises NoMethodError, returning a 500 to the user instead of handling the case. The action should guard against a missing TopicUser (create one via `TopicUser.change`, or treat it as already-unsubscribed).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil, and accessing tu.notification_level crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Direct tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change side effects

The action mutates `tu` and calls `tu.save!` directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`. As a result: `notifications_changed_at` and `notifications_reason_id` are not updated (so the topic's notification reason stays e.g. `auto_watch_category`, which is why the client route has to null out `notificationReasonText` to hide it), no `MessageBus.publish("/topic/#{topic_id}", { notification_level_change: ... })` is sent (other open tabs/clients keep showing the old state), and `observe_after_save_callbacks_for`/UserActionObserver are not run. The unsubscribe should go through `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so the same bookkeeping as the rest of the app happens.

unsubscribe_link now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking emails that don't pass it

The shared `unsubscribe_link` string was changed to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}` in addition to `%{user_preferences_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` render `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` for every message built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url:`; any other path that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without `unsubscribe_url:` will raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument` while building the message. The existing spec had to add `unsubscribe_url:` for exactly this reason. Either supply a default `unsubscribe_url` in `MessageBuilder#initialize`, or make the interpolation tolerant.

Template name does not match the topicUnsubscribe route

The route is declared as `this.route('topicUnsubscribe', { path: '/t/:slug/:id/unsubscribe' })` and has no custom `renderTemplate`/`templateName`. Ember therefore looks up the default template for route name `topicUnsubscribe` (i.e. `topic-unsubscribe`), matching the added controller and view files which use the dashed name. The template added here is `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs`, which resolves to the template name `topic/unsubscribe` (the form used for a nested `topic.unsubscribe` route). With the current route name this template will not be found, so the unsubscribe route renders no template (blank page). Rename the file to `templates/topic-unsubscribe.hbs` or provide an explicit `renderTemplate`/`templateName`.

Unsubscribe mutates state via a GET request with no CSRF protection `TopicsController#unsubscribe` changes the user's notification level but is reachable through the GET routes `t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` and `t/:topic_id/unsubscribe`, and the action is added to `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`. Rails does not apply the CSRF token check to GET requests, so a third-party page can embed `` and, for a logged-in user, silently mute that topic without their consent. The same GET also makes the action vulnerable to link prefetching/scanning by clients that try to follow links. State-changing actions reached from emails should use a confirm step or a signed/tokenized request rather than a bare GET.

No tests for the new unsubscribe behavior

The only spec change is adding `unsubscribe_url:` to an existing message-builder example; nothing asserts the new behavior. There are no specs for `TopicsController#unsubscribe` (including the nil-TopicUser case and the redirect when slug is blank), the new `t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe` / `t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` routes, `Topic#unsubscribe_url`, or the fact that the per-topic link actually appears in the rendered email body/HTML. Given the action contains a crash path and bypasses the normal `TopicUser.change` path, these paths need coverage before merge.
