true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is BSD/macOS-only and breaks on GNU/Linux

`sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses the macOS form of `sed -i`. On GNU sed (typical Linux dev boxes / CI) `-i` treats `''` as the (empty) suffix and then interprets the following expression/arguments incorrectly, so the inline replacement fails and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL is left unchanged (or the command errors). Use a portable approach (e.g. write to a temp file and move it, or detect the OS) so the script works cross-platform.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: the macOS/BSD `sed -i ''` syntax fails on Linux with GNU sed.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete-cache action shown for delegation/team credentials that the handler rejects

deleteCacheHandler authorizes solely by `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { id: credentialId, userId: user.id } })`. Delegation credentials (and team credentials with a null userId) are owned by a different user/admin, so this lookup returns null and the mutation throws "Credential not found or access denied". However, CredentialActionsDropdown only hides the remove-app action for delegation (`canDisconnect = !delegationCredentialId && ...`); it still renders the "Delete cached data" action whenever `hasCache` is truthy, and delegated Google calendars do have a cache row keyed by that credential's DB id, so `cacheUpdatedAt` is set. Result: delegated/team users see "Delete cached data" but every attempt fails with the error toast. Either authorize using the same rule that builds connectedCalendars, or hide the delete action when the credential isn't owned by the session user.

Deleting cache does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status

deleteCacheMutation.onSuccess only calls `onSuccess?.()` (= props.onChanged). Unlike disconnectMutation, which explicitly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in onSettled, the cache mutation never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. When the parent does not pass a refetching `onChanged` (it is optional in SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper), the tRPC cache retains the old `cacheUpdatedAt`, so after a successful delete the dropdown still shows "Cache Status" and "Delete cached data" until a manual page reload. Invalidate the connectedCalendars query in onSuccess/onSettled as the disconnect path does.

No test for deleteCache authorization ceiling

deleteCache permanently deletes calendar cache rows and its only safety property is the ownership check. There is no test asserting that a user cannot delete the cache of a credential they do not own (mutation should reject) and can delete their own. Given this is a destructive, authorization-gated mutation, a unit/integration test covering the not-owner rejection and the owner success path should be added before merge.

Migration backfills all existing caches with the migration timestamp

Adding `updatedAt TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` sets every pre-existing CalendarCache row to the migration run time. getCacheStatusByCredentialIds surfaces this value as "Last updated", so for the existing rows the UI will report the deploy time as the last update for up to the cache TTL (CACHING_TIME = 30 days), which is misleading. Since the real update time can be approximated as `expiresAt - CACHING_TIME`, consider backfilling with that (or leaving the column nullable for legacy rows) instead of NOW().

Unnecessary SelectedCalendar.updatedAt update with no reader

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now ends with `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`. This issues an extra UPDATE across all SelectedCalendars for the credential on every cache population (i.e. every sync/webhook), only to bump `@updatedAt`, yet nothing reads SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for display — the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt via cacheUpdatedAt. The PR notes this too. It is dead work on a latency-sensitive path; remove it (or add the consumer that justifies it).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check mishandles days off and split shifts

The new working-hours guard uses workingHours.find and returns false only when the first entry whose days includes slotStartTime.day() does not contain the slot. This has two failure modes: (1) if the user has no working-hours entry for that weekday, find returns undefined and the slot falls through as available, so fixed hosts can be booked on their days off; (2) if the user has multiple ranges on the same weekday, such as 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00, an afternoon slot is compared only against the first range and rejected even though it is within the second range. In addition, line 142 sets end equal to start instead of using slotEndTime, so a slot that starts before closing but ends after closing is not rejected. The check needs to reject missing weekday entries and test the slot against all matching ranges, including the slot end.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that line 142 sets end equal to start instead of using slotEndTime, matching the golden issue despite also reporting other working-hours bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date override interval only rejects slots wholly before or after it

The containment test rejects a slot only when slotEndTime is before/equal overrideStart or slotStartTime is after overrideEnd. It therefore accepts slots that partially overlap an override: a 13:30-14:30 slot with a 14:00-18:00 override starts before the override but ends inside and is treated as within the override; a slot starting exactly at 18:00 is also accepted because the end check uses strict isAfter. Combined with the early return on dateOverrideExist, these slots bypass normal working hours and busy checks. The condition should require slotStartTime >= overrideStart and slotEndTime <= overrideEnd. Separately, the zero-length override check at line 114 compares two Dayjs objects with ===, so a start-equals-end override is never recognized as the unavailable case.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses interval containment, it explicitly identifies the same underlying bug: comparing two Dayjs objects with === compares references and fails to recognize equal start and end values.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override path returns true before busy-time checks

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot falls inside a date override the function sets dateOverrideExist and then returns true at line 133 before the busy.every(...) check at line 153. The busy array contains the host's Cal bookings and calendar busy times. As a result, any fixed host with a date override appears free for the whole override even when already booked, so personal and round-robin events can create double bookings on override days. The override should bypass normal working-hour checks only; busy times still need to be evaluated.

Active date overrides are still selected by the override wall-clock UTC date

activeOverrides is selected by comparing dayjs.utc(override.start) directly against the invitee's local day boundaries. Date override start values are stored as wall-clock times (for example, 14:00 Asia/Kolkata is stored as 14:00Z), so this comparison works only when the organizer and invitee dates happen to align. For a large positive invitee offset such as UTC+14, an override stored at 14:00Z on the invitee day falls after the invitee day's UTC end boundary (10:00Z the same day), so the override is filtered out and the new timezone conversion is never applied. The filter should compare the converted instant or otherwise test overlap against the invitee day.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin date override fix

The PR description says fixed-host date overrides in round-robin events are fixed and should prevent bookings when the fixed host is unavailable, but the added test only changes the invitee timezone for a personal event. It has no ROUND_ROBIN event, no fixed host with a date override, and no busy booking on the override day. As a result, the regressions in checkIfIsAvailable (busy times being skipped and the working-hours filtering) are not caught. Add a scenario with a round-robin event, a fixed host whose date override restricts availability, a loose host, and an existing booking during the override.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increment is a lost-update race under overlapping cron runs

On failure, both paths write `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read before the network call. The cron endpoint has no lock or claim preventing overlapping invocations. Two runs can process the same unscheduled reminder, both call Twilio (causing duplicate SMS), and both write the same incremented value. As a result, two failures can leave `retryCount` at 1 instead of 2, so the reminder is retried more often than intended and may never reach the deletion threshold. Use an atomic update such as `{ increment: 1 }` and claim the row (e.g. conditional update or `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) before sending.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same lost-update race: incrementing retryCount from a previously read value can lose concurrent increments. Both recommend Prisma's atomic increment, and the candidate covers both failure paths as the golden comment does.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes non-SMS and already-scheduled reminders

The second branch of the cleanup `deleteMany` has only `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`. It is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` or `scheduled: false`, so this SMS cron will delete any `WorkflowReminder` with `retryCount > 1`, including non-SMS reminders if the field is used elsewhere, and including rows that are already marked as scheduled. Deleting a scheduled row drops its provider reference (for example the Twilio SID) while the provider-side message may still be queued, and it can no longer be cancelled through the normal workflow path. Add the method and unscheduled predicates to this branch.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing non-SMS reminders to be deleted. Its additional concern about already-scheduled reminders does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
Retry update failure can abort the whole reminder batch

The new `retryCount` update inside the `catch` block is not itself protected. If it fails, for example because another cron invocation already deleted the row or because of a transient database error, the exception escapes the catch, aborts the `for` loop, and prevents every remaining due reminder from being processed. The endpoint then returns 500 instead of continuing with the rest of the batch. Perform this update in its own try/catch or use `updateMany` so one stale row cannot break processing of other reminders.

Post-send database errors cause duplicate SMS sends

The `try` block wraps both `twilio.scheduleSMS` and the subsequent database update. If Twilio successfully schedules the SMS but the database update fails, execution enters this catch, increments `retryCount`, and leaves `scheduled` false without persisting `scheduledSMS.sid`. On the next cron run the same reminder is still considered unscheduled and the SMS is sent again, producing a duplicate message to the recipient. Persist the provider SID independently of the update failure, or mark the reminder as scheduled once Twilio confirms the send.

Public findMany method removed without updating consumers

This PR deletes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from `InsightsBookingService` and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which only returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment. The diff updates only this service and its tests; no other call sites are migrated. Any code that invokes `service.findMany({...})` will fail to compile (method no longer exists), and any caller that relied on the previous behavior (merging caller-supplied `where`/`select`/pagination with the authorization and filter conditions) must now build and execute its own `$queryRaw`. If such consumers exist, this is a breaking change that is not covered by the PR.

Only user-scope conditions are actually executed against the database

The single test that runs the generated SQL (`prisma.$queryRaw ... WHERE ${baseConditions}`) uses `scope: "user"`, whose authorization condition contains no array parameter. The security-critical org/team paths, which build `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})`, are only checked structurally via `toEqual(Prisma.sql...)` and never executed. Prisma array binding into `ANY($1)` has known type-inference pitfalls (e.g. requiring a cast such as `::int[]`, or failing when the array is empty). A broken/empty array binding would therefore pass this suite but throw or silently return no rows in production, which is precisely the parameter-binding risk the PR description flags.

Org-scope assertion depends on DB row ordering of team/user IDs

The org-scope test compares the service's `Prisma.Sql` to a literal with `teamIds` ordered `[org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id]` and `userIds` ordered `[user.id, user2.id, user3.id]`. The service builds those arrays from `teamRepo.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, neither of which is shown to enforce an `ORDER BY`. `toEqual` on `Prisma.Sql` compares the interpolated value arrays element-by-element, so if Postgres returns the rows in a different order the arrays differ and the test fails even though the generated SQL is semantically identical (`ANY(...)` is order-insensitive). This makes the test flaky/order-dependent rather than validating behavior; either sort the arrays before comparison or assert the query result instead.

getFilterConditions can return an unparenthesized OR fragment

For an `eventTypeId` filter, `buildFilterConditions` pushes `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` and, when it is the only filter, returns that fragment without an outer grouping (and the test at line 385 asserts this unparenthesized form). `getBaseConditions` compensates by wrapping it in parentheses, but `getFilterConditions` is a public method returning a bare `Prisma.Sql`; any other consumer that embeds it next to another `AND`/`OR` in a WHERE clause (e.g. `WHERE ${getFilterConditions()} AND ...`) would hit operator-precedence and match too many rows. Consider always returning a fully parenthesized fragment so the method is safe to compose.

Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains

The PR deletes the entire "Caching" describe block (the `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions` tests), but the service still caches results via `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` in `getAuthorizationConditions`/`getFilterConditions`. The caching paths are now untested, so a regression in cache-keying or cache invalidation would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

When the provider or sync endpoint does not return a new refresh token, this code writes the literal value `"refresh_token"` into the parsed data. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse wrapper, which is persisted as the credential key instead of the parsed token payload. Both recommend storing parsed.data or returning parsed data directly.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zoho Bigin sends credential ID as calcomUserId

`refreshOAuthTokens` expects the third argument to be the Cal.com user ID and sends it as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint. `BiginCalendarService.refreshAccessToken` passes `credentialId`, which is the internal `Credential` primary key, not `credential.userId`. The parent app will look up the wrong user and may return tokens for a different user, which are then written to this credential.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens receives credentialId instead of userId, causing incorrect user lookups at the credential sync endpoint and breaking credential synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Synced credentials do not clear the invalid flag

When an existing credential is found, the webhook only updates `key`. If the credential had been marked invalid (Google, Webex, Zoom, etc.), it remains invalid after fresh credentials are synced, so Cal.com continues to reject the newly provided valid credentials. The update should also reset `invalid` to false when new keys are supplied.

Salesforce refresh bypasses the credential sync endpoint

The new Salesforce refresh path calls `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. With `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` configured, Salesforce never asks the parent application to refresh, so the credential-sync feature does not apply to Salesforce and self-hosters relying on the parent app as source of truth still depend on local Salesforce secrets. It should use the same sync helper as the other apps or document that Salesforce is unsupported.

No tests cover the new credential-sync endpoint or refresh helpers

This PR adds a security-sensitive webhook and rewrites token refresh behavior across multiple apps without tests. Basic tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, the sync-enabled `refreshOAuthTokens` path, and the webhook update/create flow would have caught the malformed Zod schema, literal `refresh_token` injection, wrong user ID, and raw `Response` handling issues.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation promises are not awaited

In the reminder-cancellation loop, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async but are invoked inside `updatedBookings.forEach(...).forEach(...)` without `await`ing them, and the resulting promises are never collected or awaited. For EMAIL reminders the only thing that prevents delivery is the `cancelled: true` DB write performed inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`; if that floating promise has not completed when the handler returns (likely on serverless, where the lambda can be frozen right after the response is sent), the reminder stays scheduled and the email is still delivered — the exact bug this PR is meant to fix. Collect and `await Promise.all(...)` all cancellation promises before returning.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: async reminder deletion functions are called inside forEach loops without awaiting or collecting their promises, so cancellation may not complete and reminders can remain active. Its narrower focus on updatedBookings does not change the bug identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path leaves orphan WorkflowReminder rows

When `immediateDelete` is true the function cancels the send in SendGrid and returns, but it never deletes the `workflowReminder` row nor marks it `cancelled`. Callers in `handleNewBooking` (reschedule) no longer perform a separate `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany`, so for a rescheduled booking the old reminders remain in the table as `scheduled: true` rows referencing the cancelled booking until the cron's past-reminder cleanup eventually deletes them. Delete the row here (or set `cancelled`) so the DB state matches the actual SendGrid state.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same core bug: the immediateDelete path cancels the SendGrid send but leaves the WorkflowReminder database record undeleted and not marked cancelled, creating orphaned reminders. The candidate does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, but matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Reschedule reminder cleanup: try/catch is dead code and calls are unawaited

The new reschedule cleanup wraps the loop in `try { originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...) }) } catch (error) { log.error(...) }`. The callback is async and its promises are not awaited, so (a) any rejection from the cancellation calls becomes an unhandled rejection and is never caught by this `catch`, making the error handling dead code, and (b) the SendGrid cancellation / DB update may not complete before the handler finishes, so reminders for the old (now rescheduled) booking can still be sent. Additionally, passing `immediateDelete=true` for email performs an immediate SendGrid `status: cancel` POST, which is exactly the pending-cancellation behaviour (max 100 entries in `scheduled_sends`) this PR is trying to avoid, so reschedule-heavy accounts can still exhaust that limit and fail to cancel. Await the calls and consider using the mark-cancelled path for reschedules too.

requestReschedule reminder cancellation not awaited

In `requestReschedule`, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` are called inside `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach(...)` without awaiting. For EMAIL these functions only mark the row `cancelled: true`, so if the floating promise does not run before the request completes (serverless freeze), the reminder for the now-cancelled/rescheduled booking stays live and the reminder email is still sent — the bug being fixed. Await or `Promise.all` these calls.

Past-reminder cleanup deletes cancelled reminders before they can be cancelled

The handler first runs `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany({ where: { method: EMAIL, scheduledDate: { lte: now } } })` and only afterwards looks up `cancelled: true` reminders with `scheduledDate <= now + 1 hour`. Because the cleanup runs first, any cancelled reminder whose `scheduledDate` has just passed is deleted from the DB without ever being cancelled in SendGrid, so the reminder email is delivered. Since this cron runs every 15 minutes, a cancellation made within ~15 minutes of a reminder's send time (after the last cron run while the reminder was still in the future) falls into this gap and the email goes out. The cancellation pass should run before/independent of the past-reminder cleanup, and the window/cadence must guarantee every reminder is cancelled before its send time.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe requests

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased but `guest` is not, so a blacklisted address such as `evil@example.com` can be bypassed as `Evil@Example.com`. Existing-attendee checks are also case-sensitive (`guest === attendee.email`), so mixed-case duplicates can be inserted. The request schema allows duplicate emails and the handler only compares each guest to existing attendees, not to other guests in the same request, so `guests: ["a@x.com", "a@x.com"]` creates duplicate Attendee rows and can send duplicate invitations. Normalize/lowercase addresses and dedupe both against existing attendees and within the request.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same blacklist bypass: blacklist emails are lowercased but input guest emails are not, allowing mixed-case addresses to evade the restriction. The additional duplicate-attendee concerns do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner permission check uses AND instead of OR

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` requires the caller to satisfy both `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`. A normal team admin is not a team owner, so the computed value is false and the mutation returns FORBIDDEN even though the UI and variable name treat team admins as allowed. Depending on whether `isTeamAdmin` also returns true for owners, owners may fail as well. This should use OR semantics, or a helper that checks either role.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same permission-check bug: AND requires both admin and owner roles, while OR should allow either role.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails are sent using the original guests list instead of the filtered list

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the raw request array, not `uniqueGuests`. If a request contains both an already-existing attendee and a new guest, the existing attendee is treated as newly added by the email manager and receives `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of the add-guests notification. The email manager should receive only the guests that were actually inserted (`uniqueGuests`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same misclassification: the email manager checks attendees against the raw input guests array rather than only newly added guests, causing existing attendees included in the request to receive AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe requests

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is lowercased but `guest` is not, so a blacklisted address such as `evil@example.com` can be bypassed as `Evil@Example.com`. Existing-attendee checks are also case-sensitive (`guest === attendee.email`), so mixed-case duplicates can be inserted. The request schema allows duplicate emails and the handler only compares each guest to existing attendees, not to other guests in the same request, so `guests: ["a@x.com", "a@x.com"]` creates duplicate Attendee rows and can send duplicate invitations. Normalize/lowercase addresses and dedupe both against existing attendees and within the request.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the golden issue: guests are checked against existing attendees but not deduplicated within the request, allowing repeated emails to create duplicate Attendee rows. Its additional case-sensitivity concerns do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
addGuests emails ignore event type standard-email settings

`sendAddGuestsEmails` unconditionally sends organizer and attendee emails and does not accept or check `eventTypeMetadata`, unlike the surrounding `sendScheduledEmails`, `sendCancelledEmails`, etc. As a result, event types configured with `disableStandardEmails.all.host` or `disableStandardEmails.all.attendee` will still notify those users when guests are added. The handler has the event type and should pass metadata through so these settings are honored.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor EventType metadata disableStandardEmails flags, causing host or attendee emails to be sent even when standard emails are disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Any booking attendee can add arbitrary guests

The authorization check explicitly permits `isAttendee` callers to add guests. An external invitee who knows or guesses the numeric booking id can therefore append arbitrary email addresses, cause calendar invites to be sent, and trigger emails to all attendees that contain meeting details. Unless the product intentionally allows guests to invite further guests, this should be restricted to the organizer and authorized team admins/owners.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

The EventManager is constructed from `ctx.user` credentials. When the caller is a team admin/owner or attendee rather than the booking organizer, the calendar update runs with the wrong account and may fail or modify the organizer's calendar event under a different user's credentials. The handler already loads `booking.user` with credentials, so the organizer's credentials should be used for the booking's calendar update.

Guests are persisted before the external calendar update

`prisma.booking.update` inserts the new attendees before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` runs. If the calendar update throws, the API returns an error but the guest rows remain in the database. The user sees failure and retries, but the retry then reports `emails_must_be_unique_valid` because the guests already exist. This leaves the operation in an ambiguous state; calendar sync failures should be handled without committing an unreported partial update.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The new endpoint has no tests covering authorization (organizer, team admin/owner, attendee), duplicate or mixed-case email handling, blacklist filtering, or email recipient selection. These are exactly the areas where the current implementation has defects, so endpoint-level tests would both catch regressions and document the intended permissions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use enforcement is a non-atomic read-modify-write

Backup-code consumption is implemented as: decrypt the stored array, set `backupCodes[index] = null`, then `prisma.user.update` with a re-encrypted copy. This is a classic TOCTOU read-modify-write with no locking or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests that present the same backup code can both read the pre-update value, both find the code valid, and both succeed — so a single backup code can be used more than once under concurrency. Since backup codes are a recovery/second-factor credential, being able to replay one defeats the 'used exactly once' guarantee stated in the UI copy. A conditional/atomic update (e.g. compare-and-set on the ciphertext, or a DB transaction with row lock) is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same non-atomic read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same backup code before either update is persisted, allowing reuse and violating one-time-use semantics.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login can bypass password verification when a totpCode is also sent

Password verification is gated on `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), while the backup-code branch is entered whenever `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` is truthy (line 131), regardless of whether a `totpCode` was supplied. Because these two conditions are independent, a request that contains a valid backup code AND any non-empty `totpCode` value skips password checking but still goes through the backup-code validation path. The consequence is that anyone holding a single leaked backup code can log in with just that code plus a garbage totpCode, without knowing the account password — the backup code ceases to be a second factor and becomes a single factor. The UI happens to set `totpCode` to an empty string in backup mode, so this is only reachable by calling the credentials provider directly, but it is a real authentication bypass of the password requirement. The backup-code branch should also require the password (or the password check should not be skipped merely because `totpCode` is present when `backupCode` is being used).

Dismissing the dialog after enabling 2FA never calls onEnable, leaving the toggle out of sync

Previously `handleEnable` called `onEnable()` immediately on success. Now it transitions to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes`, and `onEnable()` is only invoked from the explicit 'Close' button (line 269). The `Dialog`'s `onOpenChange` (line 166) is still wired straight to the parent, so a user who dismisses the modal via Escape, backdrop click, or the close (X) button after the TOTP code was accepted leaves the server-side 2FA enabled (the enable endpoint already set `twoFactorEnabled: true`) while the parent never runs `onEnable()` / refetch, so the settings switch and related state can continue to display 2FA as disabled. The finalization should happen on any close path (or the parent should refetch on close), not only on the dedicated Close button.

No test covers the core feature: logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code

The PR description's checklist explicitly states no tests were added, and the added e2e steps only click the download and copy buttons and then close the dialog; both content assertions are left as `// TODO` and nothing exercises the actual backup-code path. The two security-sensitive behaviors this PR introduces — consuming a backup code during login (single-use invalidation) and disabling 2FA via a backup code — have zero automated coverage. Given the password-bypass and single-use race described elsewhere, the absence of a test that actually signs in with a backup code and asserts that the same code is then rejected leaves these regressions undetected. At minimum, a login-with-backup-code test (and the already-flagged 'TODO' file-content check) should be added.

Existing 2FA users have no backup codes and no way to generate them, making 'Lost access' a dead end

`backupCodes` is a new nullable column, so every user who enabled 2FA before this migration has `user.backupCodes === null`. When such a user uses 'Lost access' and submits anything, they hit `if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`, which renders `t("missing_backup_codes")` = 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' That instruction is impossible to follow: the only endpoint that creates backup codes is `setup.ts`, which returns `TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled` for users who already have 2FA on, and this PR adds no 'regenerate backup codes' UI. These users are therefore permanently locked out of the recovery path (they must disable and re-enable 2FA, which is exactly what the feature is meant to avoid). Either the message should not tell users to do something the product does not offer, or a way to generate/regenerate backup codes for already-enabled 2FA should be provided.

Exhausting all backup codes reports 'incorrect code' instead of 'no backup codes'

After codes are consumed they are set to `null` but the array (and therefore the encrypted string) is never emptied, so `user.backupCodes` remains a truthy JSON string of nulls. The guard on line 137 (`if (!user.backupCodes) throw new Error(ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes)`) never fires once all codes are used; instead `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` returns -1 and the user is told `incorrect_backup_code` forever. A user with zero remaining codes should be told they have none left (the `MissingBackupCodes` path) rather than being told each retry that their code is wrong.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Crash when Google Meet is selected without a destination calendar

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is the first element of `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, so it is undefined when the event has no destination calendar. The next condition dereferences `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` whenever `evt.location === MeetLocationType`. Previously optional chaining made this safe. Any Google Meet booking without a destination calendar now throws inside EventManager.create instead of falling back to Cal Video.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: a null or empty evt.destinationCalendar leaves mainHostDestinationCalendar undefined, and accessing its integration property causes a crash. The candidate's differing method attribution and Google Meet framing do not change the core issue.

Base CalDAV service ignores credentialId when selecting destination calendars

With multiple destination calendars, `createEvent` filters the credential's calendars by the first destination's externalId. For the second host's credential that externalId belongs to another account, so the filter produces no calendars and the method returns success without creating anything. The selection must be made using the `credentialId` passed to `createEvent` or another identifier that belongs to the current credential.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same calendar-selection logic error: using externalCalendarId/externalId can fail to select a calendar for the current credential, and selection should instead use credentialId or other credential-aware logic.

Organization slug creation is inverted for self-hosted billing settings

true_positives.golden_comment: The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stale credential reused when a reference credential cannot be loaded

In `updateAllCalendarEvents` the loop reuses the outer `credential` variable. If `this.calendarCredentials` has no match and the DB lookup fails or returns a credential without `app.slug`, `credential` still holds the previous iteration's credential or remains undefined. The code then calls `updateEvent(credential, ...)`, potentially updating the wrong calendar or failing. It should skip that reference when no credential is resolved and scope the variable per iteration.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unresolved-credential issue: when a reference's credential cannot be found, updateEvent may receive an undefined credential and fail. Its additional concern about reusing a stale credential does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Updated calendar references lose credentialId and externalCalendarId

`referencesToCreate` for `updateLocation` now reads `result.externalId` and `result.credentialId`, but `CalendarManager.updateEvent` never puts those fields on its returned EventResult. Editing a booking location therefore creates BookingReference rows with both fields undefined. Previously the `evt.destinationCalendar` fallback populated them. Later updates/cancellations may then target the wrong calendar or fail to find the external event.

Collective hosts' destination calendars are dropped when the organizer has none

`evt.destinationCalendar` is explicitly set to `null` when neither the event type nor organizer has a destination calendar. The optional push then silently does nothing, so `teamDestinationCalendars` collected from the other collective hosts is discarded. In that case EventManager never receives those hosts' destination calendars and collective hosts do not get calendar invites. The array should be initialised to `[]` before collecting/pushing team destinations.

Hangout-link patch uses undefined calendarId when destination is absent

`selectedCalendar` can be undefined when no destination calendar matches the credential, and insert correctly falls back to `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`. The follow-up `events.patch` still passes `calendarId: selectedCalendar`, so in the fallback case the patch is sent with an undefined calendar id and the generated hangoutLink is not written into the event description. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` fallback in the patch.

Office365 createEvent writes to the first host's calendar for every credential

`createEvent` ignores the new `credentialId` argument and always chooses `event.destinationCalendar[0].externalId`. When EventManager iterates collective hosts, the second host's Office365 credential is used against the first host's calendar id, causing 403/404 errors or creating the event in the wrong calendar. It needs to select the destination whose `credentialId` matches the credential passed to `createEvent`.

Lark createEvent also ignores credentialId and uses the first destination

The Lark implementation now takes the first element of `event.destinationCalendar` for every credential. For a collective booking, the second host's Lark credential will attempt to use the first host's calendarId, likely failing or writing to the wrong calendar. `createEvent` needs to choose the destination entry matching the credential it was called with.

Recurring collective cancellation only uses organizer credentials and repeats deletes

When cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, the loop over the new multiple calendar references re-enters the same block for every reference, but inside it ignores the current reference and only iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials`, deleting the first calendar reference of every updated booking. For a collective booking, second-host references/credentials are never used, so those external events remain, and the same organizer deletions are issued once per reference.

No test for collective multi-host destination calendars

The only test change updates the expected webhook shape for BOOKING_REJECTED. There is no test covering collective events with multiple destination calendars or the new create/update/delete paths, despite many calendar services and EventManager being changed. This leaves the primary regression and the calendar-service credential-selection bugs untested.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach in reschedule is not awaited and try/catch cannot catch its failures

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` starts async callbacks but does not await the returned promises. `Reschedule` can return before `getCalendar` and `deleteEvent` finish, and the surrounding try/catch is ineffective for rejections from those awaits, producing unhandled rejections and potentially leaving calendar events undeleted. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` or a `for...of` loop.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify async callbacks passed to forEach whose promises are not awaited, causing premature completion, unhandled rejections outside the surrounding try/catch, and incomplete cleanup. Both recommend for...of or awaited Promise.all with map.

false_positives.candidate:
appStore export now returns promises while most consumers still expect modules

The default export was changed from a map of module namespaces to a map of `import()` promises. Every existing `appStore[name]` access now yields a Promise unless the caller awaits it. This PR updates only a small set of call sites, so other consumers will read `.lib`, `.metadata`, or `.credentials` from a Promise and get undefined, breaking calendar, video, and payment integrations at runtime (and likely failing typecheck where the old module type is expected). Either keep a synchronous metadata map or update every consumer and the exported type to the async contract.

getCalendarCredentials now silently returns calendar promises

Because `getCalendar` became async, `getCalendarCredentials` now stores a `Promise<Calendar | null>` in the `calendar` field while remaining a synchronous function. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to await that field. Any other caller of this exported function that treats `calendar` as a Calendar will call methods on a Promise. Make the function async and await `getCalendar`, or explicitly change the return type to expose promises and migrate all callers.

requestReschedule fires calendar deletion asynchronously without awaiting it

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside an async callback that the mutation never awaits. The mutation can return before calendar/video cleanup starts or completes, and failures become unhandled rejections rather than being handled by the mutation. Collect the promises with `map` and `await Promise.all` so reschedule cleanup is reliable.

Recurring cancellation may skip calendar deletes because async forEach is not awaited

In the recurring-bookings branch, credentials are processed with `forEach(async ...)`. false_positives.candidate:
Failed work items are marked completed and committed

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, complete_offset is called in a finally block, so it runs even when result_processor raises. The exception is logged and swallowed, and the commit thread then treats the offset as successfully processed and commits it. A transient processing failure therefore loses the message instead of retrying it; the new error-handling test also expects the offset not to be committed after a processing failure.

Submit exceptions are converted into successful offsets

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing, then calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. That marks the message as processed even though no work item was queued, so the offset is committed and the message is dropped. Failures should propagate or be routed to a DLQ rather than being completed.

OffsetTracker can commit past a gap after the first commit

get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After marking offset 100 committed, all_offsets is pruned and if the remaining set is {102, 103}, start becomes 102, so the method returns 103 and commits offset 104 even though offset 101 was never added or processed. This contradicts the class's stated guarantee and the new gap test; once the first commit occurs, a missing prior offset is no longer treated as blocking.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs

Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. On the older Python versions supported by this repository, q.shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), leaving workers blocked in Queue.get() and making the join timeouts ineffective. Additionally, when a worker catches a processing exception, evaluating the except queue.ShutDown clause raises AttributeError and kills the worker thread.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each queue is created with queue.Queue() without a maxsize, and submit always enqueues immediately. If one group or worker is slow, the consumer continues pulling Kafka messages into memory without limit. The documented 'natural backpressure when queues fill up' never happens, and a slow group can cause unbounded memory growth or an OOM.

Shutdown does not drain queued work

shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Because the worker checks that flag at the top of its loop, it exits after at most the current item and leaves any remaining queued items unprocessed, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incomplete and leaves pending offsets uncommitted.

false_positives.candidate:
Changing span-buf:s keys from sets to sorted sets breaks rolling deployment

The buffer now writes span payloads with zadd and reads/merges them with zcard/zscan/zunionstore, but the Redis key namespace span-buf:s is unchanged while old deployments stored those keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deploy, old and new consumers will operate on the same keys with conflicting types: zadd/zcard/zscan on an existing set and sadd on an existing zset both raise WRONGTYPE. Unflushed segments created before the deploy will therefore fail ingestion/flushing until their TTL expires unless the keys are migrated or the namespace is versioned.

Span-count limit is no longer enforced when loading segments

The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data, and SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans is now unused; eviction is instead hard-coded to 1000 inside the Lua script. If the Python zadd pipeline writes more than 1000 spans and the following EVALSHA calls fail or the process dies between the two pipelines, the set is never evicted. Because the loader no longer rejects oversized segments, such a set can be flushed downstream. The constructor option also no longer controls anything, and its default of 1001 no longer matches the hard-coded 1000 cap.

ZUNIONSTORE default aggregation corrupts eviction scores for duplicate spans

The two zunionstore calls use the default SUM aggregation. If the same span payload exists in both the destination set and the set being merged (for example, at-least-once duplicate delivery after a parent merge), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values rather than the actual timestamp. Subsequent zpopmin eviction then treats that duplicate as newer than it really is and may evict newer spans instead. Using AGGREGATE MAX (or MIN, depending on the desired tie behavior) would preserve timestamp semantics.

Redirect-chain limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without handling deep traces

The parent-redirect walk now stops after 1000 iterations, down from 10000. For segment trees deeper than that, set_span_id will remain an intermediate span instead of resolving to the root, so later spans can be placed in the wrong segment. The change is intentional-looking but untested; if the lower bound is desired it should be justified and covered, otherwise it is a silent regression for very deep traces.

No test covers the new eviction cap or duplicate-score behavior

The PR's central behavior is eviction during insert, but every buffer test inserts at most five spans. There is no test that pushes a segment past 1000 spans and asserts that the oldest entries are evicted, no test that verifies max_segment_spans is still honored or intentionally removed, and no test for the zunionstore duplicate-member score behavior. A regression in the cap or in the removed load-time guard would pass CI.

false_positives.candidate:

_is_error_focused_query only checks whether the lowercased query contains the literal substring event.type:error. Queries such as !event.type:error, NOT event.type:error, event.type:transaction OR event.type:error, or free text containing that substring are not error-only queries, but the helper returns True. For the discover dataset this rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for queries that can include transactions or other events without sample_weight, so the response undercounts or returns zero. Top-events ordering is still based on raw count

Only the y-axis/timeseries columns are rewritten when upsampling is enabled. The top N groups are therefore selected using raw event counts while the returned series use sum(sample_weight), so the selected groups and displayed charts are inconsistent and the top groups may be wrong. Transform the orderby aggregate and count-containing equations the same way, or avoid upsampling for top-events queries.

Accidental gitlink/submodule added

The PR adds a path named sentry-repo containing only a subproject commit and no .gitmodules entry. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Ambiguous denial-cache key can collide across distinct resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example (action="a", name="b_c", parent="d") and (action="a_b", name="c", parent="d") both produce `...perm_<uid>_a_b_c_d`. Folder/dashboard UIDs and parent UIDs can contain underscores, so two distinct resources can map to the same denial key. Consequence: a denial cached for one resource is then served for a different resource the user may be allowed to access (up to the TTL). Use an unescapable delimiter or length-prefix/hash the components.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates components with underscores without escaping, which produces ambiguous or colliding keys and incorrect denial cache hits.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache is never invalidated and can re-deny newly granted (e.g. newly created) resources for 30s

The new permission-denial cache is written whenever a full DB re-query returns not-allowed (service.go:154) and is consulted at the top of Check (service.go:117) to short-circuit to `Allowed:false` without any re-validation. No code path ever deletes these keys on permission changes; they only expire via `shortCacheTTL` (30s). Consequence: once a check is denied, a subsequent grant (including the exact "creator of a just-created dashboard/folder" scenario this PR targets, e.g. a check that runs before the grant is committed) keeps returning `Allowed:false` for up to 30s, reintroducing the bug the PR is meant to fix. Also, because the cache hit is decided by key presence rather than the stored value, any future code that stores `false` under this key would still deny. Consider invalidating denial keys on permission writes (or making this cache consistent with the freshness guarantee of the allow path).

Every denied check now performs a full DB permission query

When the cached permission map is present but does not contain the requested resource, `checkPermission` returns false and Check falls through to `s.getIdentityPermissions` (service.go:139). Since the cache read inside `getUserPermissions` was removed, this path always executes a full DB query (user identifiers, basic role, teams, permissions). The only thing that prevents a DB query on a repeat denied check is the per-resource denial cache. Consequence: the first check for each distinct resource a user cannot access now hits the DB, whereas previously the cached permission map short-circuited it. For denial-heavy traffic or checks over many inaccessible resources, this is a substantial increase in DB load. Consider recording that a cached permission set is known-complete/current so genuine denials can be served without a DB round-trip.

List has no DB fallback for a stale permission map, so newly created resources are omitted

`List` only re-queries the DB when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error, i.e. when the entire per-action permission map is absent. When the map is present but stale, `List` builds its response purely from that cached map, so scopes for dashboards/folders created after the map was cached are omitted for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s). If the reported issue is observed through listing (new resource not appearing right after creation), this path remains unfixed: only `Check` received the DB fallback on a cache miss. Consider applying the same freshness handling to `List`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests each re-read the manifest

GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. On a cold cache under load this means N sequential disk reads/JSON decodes instead of one, and each request's latency is multiplied by the number of queued callers because the lock is held for the entire IO. The standard fix is to re-check the shared state under the write lock (and return it if already populated) before doing the work, or to only compute outside the lock and swap under it, so exactly one goroutine populates the cache.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw in GetWebAssets: after the read lock shows an empty cache, the write lock is taken without re-checking whether another goroutine already populated the cache. This is the incomplete double-checked locking pattern.

false_positives.candidate:
In Dev mode every request holds the exclusive write lock during file IO, serializing all callers

When `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` the early return at line 45 is skipped, so every call now takes the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds it for the whole `os.Open` + JSON decode (and potentially the HTTP round-trip to the CDN if the `cdn` branch is ever enabled). Previously concurrent dev requests read the manifest in parallel. Since dev mode intentionally re-reads on every request, a page load issuing several asset requests will now serialize them on this mutex, and a slow/failed read stalls all other callers. If the intent is to always refresh in dev, read/build the result before taking the lock and only swap the pointer (and/or use singleflight to collapse concurrent refresh work) so the critical section contains only the assignment rather than blocking IO.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
MaxCount cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained under concurrent deletes

The MaxCount cleanup is split into a SELECT that loads excess IDs at OFFSET MaxCount and a later DELETE by those IDs, with no transaction between them. If newer annotations are deleted in that window, rows selected as excess can become part of the newest MaxCount annotations but are still deleted. For example, with MaxCount=1 and annotations id=1 and id=2, cleanup selects id=1 as excess; if a user deletes id=2 before the DELETE runs, cleanup deletes id=1 and leaves zero annotations even though one should have been retained. The PR comment only acknowledges under-deletion from concurrent inserts, not this over-deletion/data-loss case from concurrent deletes.

SQLite parameter-limit test does not actually exceed the modern limit

The new test creates 40003 annotations but splits them across alert, dashboard and API annotation types, so each per-type cleanup batch fetches at most about 13335 IDs. The configured batch size is 32767, but the actual DELETE statement never contains more than about 13335 IDs. On SQLite >= 3.32.0 the variable limit is 32766, so this test would still pass even if deleteByIDs used placeholders instead of inlining the IDs. It therefore does not exercise the >32767-ID case named by the test; create more than 32767 annotations of a single type or test deleteByIDs directly.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit request context and are canceled when the request ends

Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection start legacy writes in goroutines using the handler's request context. Go's HTTP server cancels that context as soon as ServeHTTP returns, so these goroutines will frequently begin with an already-canceled context and the legacy write will fail immediately. The 10-second timeout added inside the goroutine does not help because its parent is already canceled. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (to preserve values such as user/tenant) or a writer-scoped background context before spawning the goroutine.

Async legacy writes are unordered and can overwrite newer state

Each write spawns an independent goroutine with no sequencing. Two successive updates to the same object can reach legacy storage out of order, and an update can run before the create that preceded it. Legacy storage can therefore end up with older data than unified storage even when both operations succeed, which defeats the purpose of the safety copy. This needs ordered delivery (for example a per-object or per-resource queue) or a different fallback strategy.

Legacy update recomputes the update from the legacy object instead of using the stored result

Storage.Update computes the new object by calling objInfo.UpdatedObject against the unified-storage old object. The async legacy path then passes the original objInfo again, so Legacy.Update calls UpdatedObject against the legacy store's old object. For patches/applies or any UpdatedObjectInfo that depends on the current object, the two stores can produce different results and diverge. The previous implementation explicitly wrapped objInfo with the object returned from unified storage; this path should pass a wrapper carrying the storage result (res) instead of the raw objInfo.

Async legacy write failures are silently dropped

The async Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection goroutines only feed legacy errors into a metric; no log is emitted. If legacy writes fail because of context cancellation, validation, conflicts, or storage errors, operators get no explicit indication that unified and legacy storage have diverged. At least log the error with kind/name and the fact that it occurred on the async legacy path.

The error case for TestMode3_Create configures setupLegacyFn to return an error, but mode 3 calls Storage.Create first. There is no expectation set for the storage mock, so the test will panic on an unexpected mock call instead of exercising the intended storage-error path. This case needs setupStorageFn returning the error (and should leave legacy unconfigured because it should not be called).

Delete and DeleteCollection tests spawn async legacy calls that are neither mocked nor awaited

TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection only configure storage expectations. On success, mode 3 launches a goroutine that calls d.Legacy.Delete or d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but the legacy mock has no matching expectation and the test does not wait for the goroutine. That leads to a panic from testify's mock (often asynchronously) and the assertions do not verify that the legacy write happened at all. The tests need legacy mock expectations plus a synchronization mechanism (or an injectable executor) for the async operation.

Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy propagation

The new mode-3 cases run the shared doPlaylistTests helper, which creates/updates via the Kubernetes API and then immediately lists or gets the same data through the legacy API and requires exact equality. Mode 3 intentionally writes to legacy asynchronously, so legacy may not have caught up yet and the test will be flaky or fail. These checks need eventual-consistency polling or should not assert immediate legacy visibility for mode 3.
